A It:MY SIINSET. That evening we looked at the sunset golden, That pathway of light o'er'the western sea, -And you sang me a rhyme from a legend olden, ' That youth and love like that path should Le: ""-- Together we gazed on the summer ocean, = Where dancing ripples but kissed its breast, No breeze awoke to ruffle its motion, .. No storm arose to disturb its rest. Soft was the warmth of the sunset,splendour, With its magicetintings of crimson light, Our hearts were true, and our words grew tender, I-, As the world around us was glad and bright; Too soon from our gaze the sun had vanished, Too quickly the glory had changed to gray, •The gleam of light from the sea was banished, And gone was the glow of that summer day. Oh. type of youth, that is fair and fleeting! Oh, fading vision of joy and light! 'Oh, evening sunset! for aye rem ating, -"Youth yields to age as the day to night." True love alone has a life immortal, That perishes not in Time's rapid. tide; So we gaze in hope to the far-off portal Where the sours deep faith will be glorified. ---,The Girl's Owe Paper. - "-NM.
GROWN-UP LAND. "Good morrow, fair maid, with lashes brown, Can you tell me the way to Womanhood Town?"

• "Oh, this way and that way, never a stop. • 'Tis picking ub stitches grandma will drop, 'Tis kissing the baby's troubles away, 'Tis learning that cross words never will pay, 'Tis helping mother, 'tis sewing up rents, 'Tis reading and playing, 'tis saving the cents, • 'Tis loving and smiling, forgetting to frown, Oh, that is the way to Womanhood Town!" !.. "Just wait, my brave lad, one moment, I pray, Manhood Town lies where? Can you tell the way?" "Oh, by toiling and trying we reach that land— A bit with the head, a hit with the hand! 'Tie by climbing up the steep hill Work, 'Tis by keeping out of the wide street Shirk, 'Tis by always taking the weak one's part, 'Tis by giving the mother a happy heart, ' 'Tis by keeping bad thoughts and actions down, Oh, that is the way to Manhood Town !" And the lad and the maid ran hand in hand To their fair estates in Grown-up Land. —Leeds ifercu)y. '

One evening, after a dusty day's work at the sorting-table, I wandered down a a dong,a," out by the low hills towards the Vaal, with any gun, to try and shoot a corm or something for .supper. I saw no corans, but I -Shot a hare, some of -which we ate, and told Piet that he might have what -remained. He was usually voracious enough; but this time he made a grimace indicative of repugnance, and -gravely announced that he wanted something else, as he could not eat hare. For some time he would not tell us what objection he had to that animal, but after much urging he told us the following tradition :—"The moon -comes, by-and-by it dies, and then it comes to life again. The moon once called the hare, and. said to him: 4Go to men, and tell them that, as I die And. come to life again, so shall they also die and come-to, life again.' The hare went accordingly as he was told. and when he returned the moon asked him: 4 What did you say?' The hare replied: 'I have told them that as you die and come not to life again, so shall they also die and come not to life again." What,' said the moon," did you say that?' And being angry, he took up a stick, and hit the bare on the mouth, which became slit." tThere- fore, according to Piet, no Hottentot will eat hare, because he brought the wrong message, and was thus -the cause.of death. D— kept a thermometer hung up on a nail which was driven into one of the ridge-poles of the tent, and the mercury in the tube and bowl much exercised the mind of Piet. He asked us frequently what it was /or, aiiii eridently regarded our explana- tions as to the:use. of the instrument as mere subter- fuges designed to disguise the truth, asking: "What the use of suclething ? S'pose I see cloud die side over star, den met knew rain soon catch dis part and make plenty cold. S'pose you no able for tell if day hot or cold without dm ting ?" The word "mercury," toss he considered a slang name we had invented to describe the metal in the bowl; and one day, when D— happened to refer to it as " quicksilver " in Piet's presence, I could see a sudden gleam of intelligence in the boy's eyes, and a pleased expression on his fiat countenance, as if be had at last received corroborative .evidence of a fact. wtich he had long suspected. Next slay we came back from the claim somewhat earlier than was our custom on account of the unusual heat, and svlien D— went, asx,sual, towards the thermometer to see what the temperature was, behold no thermometer was there! We, of course, suspected Piet at once, and searched high and low for him. He was nowhere pear our tent, but after sometime we discovered him at a lit lie distance, crouched down behind a heap of "stuff " near a sorting-table, busily engaged with something on the ground. We approached him on tip-toe, and beheld an amusing sight. Before him on the ground lay the broken thermometer, and beside it in the dust, was a glistening little silver globnle of mercury. Pietai eyes were fastened upon this with a ` mingled expression of amazement and fright. Every now and then he would cautiously extend a finger and thumb and endeavour to pick up the mercury, which naturally escaped him, and roiled to one side. His action and expression each time he found he had missed it were so absurd, that at last we could not restrain our laughter; he at once heard us, looked round, and the next moment was dancing about and making grimaces at us two hundred yards off. It was not until the pangs of hunger compelled him, towards the evening, to approach -the tent, that we caught him. Re expressed contrition, but seemed to think, at the name time, that we bad played rather a shabby trick on buril: "What for you tell me that silver livn in dem ting i ?" he asked. 'Why you no say it witchcraft, and then I left him. That no good silver—not money silver." —Ail the Year Round. '

I' streeams up tort Market th' creawd clusters an.g( sae, For bizness, an pleshur, an gam; Thera o sooarts together—owd age wild stick; An youth, limber, lithesum, an breet ; . Thers t' rich, an there t' needy—fooak healthy an sick, , Mixed i' th' rook every Satterda neet. On th' Market Place butchers o sheawt thersels hooarse,, But th' fish chaps they bawl a deal woes; An th' newspaper lads gie ther cries wi fuR fooarce, While th' pot sellers jabber an case. Thers a mixtur o' o sooarts o' ear-split tin dins, I An voices a long way fro sweet; An th' rattlin o' pots, blent wi t' clatterin o' tins, Meks quare music o' t' Satterda neet. There t' nook-lurkin sponge, cadgin' hard for a gill, Wi a face like a hawf-worried ham; An tramps, as smell strongly o' leatterheyd swill, Implore as yo wernd let ern clam: Thers foo's, drunken silly, as scatter ther brass, Stannin "Sam," for o' th' fooak as they meet, I They're never content till they've melted i' th'glast Ther week's wages o' t' Satterda' neet. Thera t' widow, ate getten her thilder to bed Buys in, wi' a rayther leet pose; Thers t' couple, as hesnd bin varra long wed, Wastin brass to buy th' babby a hose. Thers t' chap, wi his sheep heyds, uts beawn to mek broth, Bundles up them an' th pot-posies reet ; An laffs to see th' antics o' weyvers i' cloth Actin swells ov a Satterda neet. Thers t' chap tekkin th' wife reawnd to buy a new shawl: An hey! wod a smile her face wears! Thers t' child, bea wt a hawp'ny, as knows heaw to bawl, Blobberin " toffy !" wi sobbin an tears. There t' hearty owd cock, as is three score an ten, , Strong an weel fro his creawn to his feet; -Shakin hands wi owd mates, he s bin droppin on, when Lookin reawnd ov a Satterda neet. Tilers gret gigglin lasses, wi moor noise than wit, I Choosin ribbins and fol-de-lols fine; An fast fella lads,—actin like they d bin hit,— Slip i' vaults, till they ged far "o'er th' line." An there t' pictur as meks th' heart feel cowd into th' chest— Its tbad shameful an sorrowful sect. 0' slovenly wimmin wi childer at th' breast, Scrawlin hooam drunk o' th' Satterda neet. Thers good an' thers bad—an' indifferent an' o, I Mixed together, wi' baskets an' bags; Thers faces uts smilin', an' sum pale wi' woe, There broadcloth, an' fustian, an' rags! There plenty wi' money, an' odd uns uts nooan, Wi' no stockins nor shoonto ther feet, Ther piteous looks wod melt th' heart ov a stooan, Dornd forged 'em o' t' Satterda neet! There t cooarters as ta.wk, o so iovin' ant kind, There ruff uns as fo eawt an felght ; Thers th' owd-fashun'd lot, to good bargains ne'er blind, As stroll reawnd late on for ther meyt. There Jews, an' there Gentiles, there "angels" an' foos ; Thers clap-trap, an' fraud, an' deceit; An' honest fooak plenty, look reawnd when yo choose, Bi th' market o' t' Satterda neet.

OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY.

Business in the House of Commons proceeded a little quieter this week. The Government have considerably modified the Irish Land Bill, which both sections of the Opposition are now anxious to see passed. It is not perfect, but, thanks to the sturdy attitude of the Opposition, it will prove a distinct advance in favour of the tenant. So anxious have the Irish members been not to stand in the way of the bill, that they have postponed their in- tention to protest against the absolutely indefensi- ble procedure of proclaiming the whole of Ireland. This will follow as soon as the bill is through. An addreas to the Crown praying for the limitation of the Tory privilege will be inoved. Of course it will not be carried, but it will bring into fuller light the arbitrary conduct of the Conservatives, backed up as they are by the Dissentient Liberals. Some of the counties that have been proclaimed are, accord- ing to the impartial testimony of the returns, much more free from crime than any county in England. But, to save time and trouble, and to preserve the ominous unanimity, the whole of Ireland is pro- claimed, and the liberty of individual citizens is at the mercy of Mr. Balfour. In the meantime it is curious to note that the Government majority is permanently decreasing. During this week it has been reduced as low as eleven and, again to twenty., Pairing is going on as fast as can be accomplished, though the Conserva- tive whips do all in their power to prevent their men taking that step. At any night may now be seen comparatively crowded Opposition Benches, whilst there are notable gaps in the ranks of the Ministerialists, though this does not mean that the latter have permanently disappeared. They remain in and about the precincts of the House ready to rush in at the sound Of the bell, and out-vote the Opposition. Mr. Chamberlain, who has not of late been constant in his attendance,qurns up now more frequently, and Lord Hartington generally spends an hour or two on the Front Bench. He received a damaging snub the other night when he backed up Mr. Smith in the stupid proposal to refuse to accept Dr. Tanner's apology. The Speaker in a brief but telling speech, delivered with admirable taste, en- tirely justified the Opposition, and brought a dis- creditable scene to a close. Another incident was the difference of opinion, somewhat hotly expressed, between Lord Randolph Churchill and Mr. Cham- berlain on one of the clauses of the bill! This greatly delighted the Irish members, as showing how limited is the bond of union between these two hot-beaded .politicians, The election at Northwich is looked forward to ' with extreme interest. It will be a typical test of public opinion. It 1885 the Liberal candidate won the seat by a thousand votes. Last year, after Mr. Gladstone hoisted the flag of Home Rule in Ireland, the Conservative won by nearly half that number. This is a considerable majority to overturn. But I Liberals are full of confidence. If the seat is re-1 gained it will be a terrible blow to the Tories andl their allies, It will show that, upon further reflec- tion and fuller knowledge, an important section of the Liberals have returned to their allegiance. The Ministerialists do not mean to leave any stone unturned to barricade their position, and we may expect to witness lively proceedings. The Jubilee time is now really over, the Naval Review, its last development, proving not the least successful of the long series. This is Goodwood week, after the close of which no one with a character to lose in society would be seen in Lon- don. The Queen forthwith retires to Balmoral, and will not again visit London this year. There is in some quarters a little apprehension arising out of the silence maintained by her Majesty with res- pect to the disposition of the .270,000 that remains of the Women's Jubilee offering after the expendi- ture on the Prince Con Sort's Statue. It. was ex- pected that the Queen's intention on the subject would have been announced to the ladies assembled to present the colossal purse. But no sign has been made, and the hospitals and other, charitable insti- tutions that conceive they have some interest in the matter are losing hope. As to Lord John Manners, though rumours offhis • approaching resignation are always contradicted, very little hope is entertained in political circles of his return to official life. He is not quite's° old as he looks, being only in his sixty-ninth year. But his health has for some time showed signs of break-- ing up, and if he were to yield to various warnings he would not delay his final retirement. But his colleagues In the Ministry are really loth to part with him. He is not a conspicuously able man, whether as an administrator or as a member of ear- Bement. But he casts about the Treasury'Bench

,that air of aristocratic birth and manner which is felt to be so sorely needed. He is a prince among those gentlemen of England" with whom it is Mr. Chamberlain's pride in these latter days to asso 'ciate. He is exceedingly popular on both sides, the older generation of members regarding him with something like personal affection. He is a striking and picturesque link with the far past, when the' young England party throve and the 'late Mr, Dis- raeli wore ringlets and festooned his brightly hued waistcoat with chains of gold. Lord John has not a precise parallel in political life, and, though he has now come to be chiefly ornamental, his col- leagues and the Conservatives as a party will not willingly let him go. Public opinion is very properly shocked at Mr. Labouchere's theatrical, party at Pope's Villa last Sunday. But as it proved an unqualified success I am afraid Mr. Labouchere Will not be disturbed by the censure which, he observes, comes exclusively from people who were not invited. How it came to pass that the performance took place on the Sun- day I explained last week. It was originally fixed for Saturday afternoon; in forgetfulness of the coun- ter aaractions of the naval review. When these made themselves felt the date was hastily altered from Saturday afternoon to Sunday evening. One of the consequences of this was that Mr. Burnand, who was to have played a part in the piece, was not able to come. Mr. Whistler was another absentee The acting on the whole was capital, the scene unique, and the audience delighted. The latter was not the least Attractive feature of the occasion It was a wonderfully mixed gathering of the best knoitm people in London. Lord Charles Beresford's escapade on the Queen's yacht last Saturday has greatly amused the public. It was eminently characteristic of him. He wanted to Communicate with his wife in a neighbouring ship, and he went about doing so in the least cir- cumlocutory manner. But id signalling from the Queen's yacht he committed a grave breach of eti- quette, and has marked his own sense of it by re- signing his office. The Queen, it *well known, is a great stickler for serious and exact observation of etiquette: but no one supposes that she will ac- cept Lord Charles's resignation. It would be fl ,great • loss to the Ministry, the noble lord being head and shoulders above the mediocrity of ministers. He will be forgiven for his high crime and misdemea- nour, and will, it is to be trusted, be more careful Ii the future.

THE CASs INQUIRY.—The official inquiry Into the cir- cumstances attending the arrest of Miss Cass by police. constable Pndacott was resumed at Scotland Yard on MOD- day morning. It was stated thit the man Reevee, who was to give evidence on behalf of Endacott, was still undiscover- able. Mr. Grain (for Miss Cass) proposed to recall the foreign lady who described'herself as Madame Pietre, who entered the cowl in a state of intense excitement. . She de- nounced Mr. Grain in bitter terms for having defamed her character, causingher to lose her Situation and het apart- ments. She'said she would bring an action againet him, , and tell people what she,knew of him. When ebe had at length calmed down Mr. Grain asked whether she had evpr represented herself to he the wife of a detective. She re- plied that she had never been married. She had never been called Picard. A witnesa named Edgar Walford, a draper's Assistant, said he saw Miss Cass faken into custody. Ho had, seen her quietly walking along the street. She did not take bold of any gentleman, nor did she speak to anyone neither was any otber.person with her. -Enrico:Mt was re- called for the purpose of pointing out the exact place where be arrested Mies Cass. He raid the arrest took place in Regent-street, and not in Oxford-street, is stated by Miss Casa and the witness Watford. Mr. Superintendent Draper. in answer to Sir Charles Warren, said every effort hid been made to find the fair woman alleged to have been with Mies Cass, but she could not be found. Some liartber evidence having been given the inquiry Was again adihntned. On Tuesday, upon the resumption of the Cass kquiry at Scot- land Yard, Police-constable Dyer was called to testify re- epectieg the exact spot at which the arrest took place, but his evidence added nothing material to the previous evi- dence.—Mr. Smith, the assessor, having expressed regret at the unwillingness shown by persons to come forward, Sir Charles Warren declared the inquiry concluded unless be- fore he made his report to the Home Secretary important evidence one way or the other was brought to his know- ledge, in which case he would give due notice to all con- cerned.

The following places are proclaimed undet clause C of sub-section 3 of section 29 of the 'Act, :—Dublin'City, Cork City, Limerick City, Water- Ford City, Kilkenny City, Galway Town, Droglo.:da Town, Carrickfergus Town, Belfast Borough, and Londonderry Borough. Mr. and Mrs. Davitt visited Bodyke on Sunday, where medals and sums of from £3 to ES were presented to the women and young girls who offered resistance to ! the sheriff and police at the recent evictions on Colonel O'Callaghan's estate at. Killaloe. On the journey from Nenagh, Mr. Devitt, who travelled with his wife on a car, was presented with an address from the people at , Killaloe. Mt. Davitt, in his reply, referred to the Land Bill, I and said the offer which had been made by the Govern- I ment towards a settlement of the question justified the course which had been taken by Mr. Parnell and himself. He felt sure that if the national spirit of the country con- tinued, the efforts they were making would cause legalised oppression and robbery to be at an end. Continuing, he said that in their struggle against the Crimes Act he was sure :they would show to the civilised axorld that they were riot going 63 siannit to uneOnStiturional interfer- Slice With their:rights as citizens of a civilised canntry: The struggle at Bodyke had , made the name of 13edylce respected, not alone in Ireland, but through the whole, world. The action of the people of Bodyke had put terror into the hearts of theorack-renters, and if other tenantry imitated their example there would be an end to evictions.—Mr. Davitt subsequently addressed, at Bpdyke, a 'meeting at length, speaking strongly against any compromise. For his part he would like to See the prisons of Deland filled:under the Crimes Act with the , manhood of the country. .

MURDERED FOR A PENNY. A SHOCKING BTORY2' The Parisian William Sikes must be given the palm over his Whitechapel colleague in Crime for cold-blooded ferocity and unmitigated barbarity. The London rough would no doubt do a murder cheaply enough, but it is hardly probable that even in the moments when be was most down on his luck" he Would go so far as to slay Nancy for the mtgerable sum of one penny. Yet this was the price paid te a miserable'voyou named Marellin by one of his companions in ruffianism for having thrown a drunken woman into the Seine, where she was drowned. The facts of the horrible case are these. A few to. lithe 1 ago the dead body of a young woman was fished up out of that part oft he river between the .Pont Saint-Michel and the Morgue. 'She was identified as a Street. girl named Levot, aged twenty - nine years, and known iii the nefarious neighbourhood of the Place Maubert as "La Bretonne." The police came to the conclusion that the woman had been thrown io, and they were right, for, thanks to the astuteness of M. Clement. a commissaire or inspector charged with crimi- nal investigations, who is worthy of the best days of the Rue Jerusalem, the murderer was tracked to his lair. It appears that a short time ago a man named Decouard was arrested, with five others, for a robbery cornmitted in the Centml`Markets. In examining the prisoners M. Clement discovered that Decouard had been the so-called protector of the unfortunath woman styled "La Bretonne." Taking the bull by the horns, M. Clement at once charged the robber with her murder. Decouard pale, became embarrassed, and finally told the officer what he knew. He said that a few hours before the murder he had been with " La.Bretonne" and several "corner boys" of his own class in a low house of enter- tairunent, the name of which was the "Café of Damp Feet" It was one of those fellows who committed the murder, but M. Clement only found him last week at Montreuil. This Marcelin had left the Café des Pieds Humides with his companions, when he suddenly offered to bet a champoreau—or cup of coffee and brandy, worth two souis—that he would throw "La Bretonne" into the Seine. The bet was accepted, and Marcelin walked to- wards the woman, who was leaning drunk against the St.'Michael Bridge. The night was dark and rainy, and ' the bridge was deserted, save by the band of rascals who watched the proceedings of their cppain with diabolical interest. Marcelin seized tho girl as if to embrace her, and then, lifting her in his arms, flung her into the dark flowing river. The splash caused the night watch- men and two policemen to run towards the spot, but they did not• see the band of ruffians. The body was found two hours afterwards. Marcelin, when he and his friends were at a safe distance from the-scene of the murder, coolly claimed his wager, and, after having SI swallowed his pup of poisonous champoreau with con- summate relish, he actually went back with his friends to see the body of the woman. Bending over the corpse was a friend of the deceased, who kissed her; but, as she was engaged in doing so, Marcelin struck her on the head, and hissed in her eat that, he would "give her a cold water bath," too, if she did not keep her tongue quiet. Mt the band are now in the bands of the police.

The quarterly general meeting of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce took place at Manchester, on Mon- day. The President (Mr. Gaddrim) said the Canadian Legislature appeared to be moving in the direction of Protection. The new tariff levied higher duties on iron and English manufactured goods; and he feared that the result would be that another market would be: not closed, at least seriously intarfaed wirb,

The 18th annual demoristrat ion of the Durhain Miners' Association was held on Durham racecourse on Satur- day. The attendance was estimated at fully 5D,000 per- sons. Speeches were delivered 'by Mr. Fenwiek, M.P., and Mr. Atherley Jones, M.P., the former dwelling on the benefits of unionism In trade, and the latter referring at length to the inquiry into the arrest of Miss Cass, and condemning the method in which the investigations were conducted, whereby insinuations against Miss Cass's character were allowed to be made without cheek. The only competition at Wimbledon on Saturday was that for the Royal Cambridge Challenge Shield between sections of regular cavalry, y ho, in the course of a ride. of three-quarters of a mile, dismounted and fired two dis- tances. The shield and £25 Were won by the 14th Hus- sars, and £l5 by the Ist Dragoons. In the evening the Duchess of Albany presented the prizes to the successful' competitors in the pavition enclosure. The Queen's prize. man, Lieutenant Warren, of the Victories, and the Prince of Wales's primman, Private Gillies, of Canada, were heartily cheered, as also were the other Canadians. the Cape team, and the English Twenty and the English Eight. CoNFYssioli OF MITRDER.—EXTRAORDINARY STORY.— yVallis Jenkins, grocer's assistant, who two years ago Fas sentenced to 15 years' renal servitude for causing the death of his employer, Mr. William Smith, Llanga- felach-street, Swansea, has ' addressed a letter from Chatham Prison to Mr. Glasbrook Richards, soli- citor, confessing his guilt in a ' tragic affair, Yglilch created a great sensation at the time, and was involved in deep mystery. The culprit was diseovered in one room on the premises shot in the - breast, whilst. his master Was found in another, on the floor, quite 'deed. The young convict stattis that at :the time lie was labouring under great difficulties, and was studying for examination to he 'admitted to Bristol College, so that he miglii'd'evotellis life to missionary work in Africa. He had domestic afflictions, and his health completely • gave way, and his mind became de- ranged, leading him to commit the rash act. Platuotrale :awn FRIENDLY SOCIETTES.—Od Satlirday afternoon a fully-attended meeting of the'comtnittee and supporters of the recently-formed Friendly Societies' Reform Association was held at Camberwell, London, "to tonsidet what Steps should be taken in view of the discussion in the House of commons last Wednesday and the remarks of the Chancellor' of the Exchequer, which t were in favour of an amendment of the Friendly Socie- fatties' Act, to obtain a reform in the management of friendly eocieties." The chair was taken by Mr. Thomas , Teesdale (Camberwell vestryman, member of the Execu= tive of the Sons Of Phcenix, of the Ancient Order of Foresters, and chairman of the executive of the new association). The honorary secretaries were Instructed to write to Mr. Gosehen. asking him to appoint a day to receive a deputation. It was arranged that members of the association should attend the lobby of the House of Commohs in the ensuing week to give practical informa- tion to any, honourable members favourable to. this movement. . ACCIDENT TO A ROYAL PARTY.—The ceremony of launching the new lifeboat presented to Bembridge, Isle of Wight, by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution, was performed on Monday by the Duchess of Edinburgh, on -behalf of the Princess Ileatrice,, who was absent, through indisposition. The, Duchess arrived in the Al.))erta about half-past two, accompanied by Prince. • Henry of Battenbera and the young tPrineatAlfred of Edinburgh. Their Royal Highnesses were received by Sir Edward Birkbeck, M.P., and the committee of the , ninstitution. Sir Edward formally handed the boat over • o the local committee, and the Duchess, having named tthe vessel "The Queen Victoria," it was launched with the crew and Prince Alfred on board. Their Royal Highnesses afterwards proceeded to qxamine the lifeboat house. and had hardly left the stage which had been erected for their acconnnbdatiOn when the structure „Suddenly collapsed, precipitating many of those upon it into the water, which, fortunately, was very shallow. No one was seriously 'hurt. The Royal party, after in, specting the boat-house, returned to Osborne. ' _ A GOOO STORY OF A STEAM FIAIHMER.—The German papers continue to publish numerous anec- dotes of the late Herr Krupp. The Vienna Extrablatt gives the following 'interesting incident, 'which marked the visit of the Emperor William to the Essen works:— The Emperor displayed great interest in the working of the. steam hammer, and Tlerr Krupp took the opportunity of speaking in high praise of the workman who had special charge of it. " Ackermann has a sure eye," he said, "and can stop the falling hammer at any moment. A hand might be placed on the anvil without fear, and he would stop the hammer within a hair's breadth of it." "Let us try it," said the Emperor, "but not with a , "human hand—try my watch," and he laid it, a splendid specimen of work richly set with brilliants, on, the 'anvil. Down came the immense mass of steel, and Ackermann, with his hand on the lever, stopped it just the sixth of an inch from the watch. When he went to hand it back, the Emperor replied kindly, "No, Acker- mann, keep' the watch in memory of an interesting moment." The workman, embarrassed, stood with out. stretched hand, not knowing what to do. Krupp came forward and took the watch, saying, "I'll keep it for you if you are afraid to take it from his Majestsy:" A ' few minutes later they again passed the spot, and Krupp • said, "Now you can take the Emperor's present from my hand," and handed Ackermann the watc& wrapped i !-AID n a thousand-mark note.

FOREIGN NEWS.
THE AFGHAN BOUNDARY SETTLEMENT. -RUSSIA'S ATTITUDE TOWARDS INDIA AND ENGLAND. •

ST. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY.—The English Commissioners left yesterday for England. Sir West Ridgeway will re- turn to India after a short stay, in England. Captain Barrow will resume his post in tile Intelligence Depart- ment in London. The Russian Commissioner, M. Lesser, will soon go to Liverpool as consul, and M. Kuhlberg will within two months return to the Caucasus.

• VIENNA. MONDAX.—TIIO Political Correspondence pub- lishes intelligence front St. Petersburg, stating that the Anglo-Russian arrangement concerning the Afghan Frontier is regarded there as the precursor of a rap- prochement in European quarters. Also, it, is added, that the Czar personally intervened in boundary negotiations.

Sr. Prranser no, MONDAY.—AIt hough the Russian press has not yet taken thn trouble to inquire into the de- tails of the settlement of the Afghan frontier, it hastens, with its usual recklessness and vanity, to couple its settlement with Turkey's rejection of the Egyptian Con- vention on the boast that Russia has triumphantly de- feated British diplomacy on two important fields.

ODESSA, MONDAY NMl:M.—Several leading articles in the South Russian press discuss the new prospect of a better understanding between England and Russia in the East. It is contended in some of the papers that the two countries which have enormous interests both in the West and in the East have much to gain from the estab- lishment of more friendly relations. • THE BULGARIAN THRONE.—A DOUBTFUL SITUATION.

CONSTANTINOPLE, SUNDAY INIGHT.—To-day the Porte is despatching to its representatives abroad new instruc- tions, theobject of which is to suggest to England, Ger- many, and Austria, that they should approach Russia and 'Ranee in the matter, and seek to obtain their con- sent to Prince Ferdinand's accession to the throne. Such craven or juggling diplomacy is not calculated to assauge the exasperation of the impatient Bulgarians, and it is not surprising that, accor ling to a telegram re- ceived this morning from Sofia, preparations are already being comme3lced there to proclaim the independence of Bulgaria. This important step, however, will not be taken for another week or two, as the Bulgarian authori- ties desire first to await the reply of the Porte. If the latter proves vague they will request. Prince Ferdinand to take the first boat down the Danube to Rustchuk and assume the crown to which he has been elected. In the event of his refusal, the proclamation of Bulgaria as an independent principality or kingdom will immediately follow.

VIENNA, MONDAY NIGHT.-It is now declared on trust- worthy authority that although the Bulgarian deputation left Vienna in the belief that Prince Ferdinand would rei sign his candidature he still remains in communication with the Bulgarian Govprnment, and doeS not Consider that the matter is at an end. On the contrary, his con- nections are actively at work negotiating with the Powers on his behalf. He is not the man, we are assured, to give up his cause on account of difficulties in his way —difficulties, moreover, which he himself foresaw.

THE BULGARIAN QUESTION. CowsrawnworLu, TIISSDAT ETENING.—The Bulgarian Government continues its representations with the object of inducing the Porte, as the suzerain Power, to come to a decision regarding the election of Prince Ferdinand to the Bulge, ian Throne. M. de Nelidoff has made a communica- tion to the Porte concerning the Bulgarian question, the tenour of which has not, however, yet transpired.

div.p: MISCELLANEOUS,

The debate on the Crofters Bill was adjourned, in order to arrange a new amendment which would settle a difference between the Lords and the Commens on the question of arrears of rent. The Markets and Fairs (Ikighing of Cattle)Bill passed through Committee, and The House adjourned at 3 25 B.M.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.JLWEDNispAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.JLWEDNispAy.

_ The Speaker took the chair at 20 minutes past twelve o'clock. 'LURING DOWN A PLACARD.—Mr. 'BRADLATION asked the Attorney-General for Ireland to state to the House the Biecific words from the Windgay placard (produced on Tuesday by the Chief Secretary) which, in his opinion, made the placard an illegal document, and justified its des- truction by the police.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRE- LAND replied that it was the duty of the re lice in the dis- trict to remove such a placard, and the action of the ser- geant in tearing it down was approved by the district in- speritor, who knew the circumstances of the district. The language of the placard might be regarded as inflammatory and tending to social disorder and breaches of the peace. He saw no reason for questioning the action of the police. He read part of the placard, which urged the people to band themselves together under the banner of the National League to prove that vercion had no terrors for them.—Mr T D. SULLIVAN asked if a newspaper circulating in the district was liable to seizure for containing the language of the plafard.—The Arroam-Gxtrgitar, for IRELAND said each case would be judged on the facts. THE bass LAND Buri.—The House went into Commit- tee on the Irish Land Bill, and on the fourth clauso Mr. T. M. BELLY said it was so bad that it outweighed all the benefits of the bill, and he would rather lose the measure . than have it passed with this clause in it.—after further . hostility to the clause had been expressed, Mr. BALFOUR said he did not think he had gone too far on the previous night in saving that Irish members were hesitating whether they should not destroy the largest measure of relief ever offered to Irish tenants, simply because it contained a clause which would cheapen a legal process to the landlord, but which would at the came time benefit the tenant and pro• mote law and order.--An Lmendment to the clause was ulti- mately lost by a majerity of 56,—Mr. M HEALY was speak- ing in support of another amendment at a quarter to six c'clock, when, in accordance with the Standing Orders, protress wasreported. Miscumatexous.—The Liquor Traffic (Local Veto) (Uls- ter) Bill, which stood for second reading, was Athdrawn.-- I The Agricultural Labourers' Holdings (Scotland) Bill was read a second time.—Mr. Haldane brought In a bill to I amend the Settled Land Act of 1882, and Sir Borthwick ! a bill to amend the law of libel. I The House adieurned at five minutes to six o'clock.

HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack short- ly after four o'clock. ALLOTMENT AND COTTAGE OARDENS.—The second read- ing of the Allotments and Cottage Garden Compensation Bill was moved by the Earl ef Witscirusza and NOTTING- HAM, who had charge of the bill in the House of Commons when sitting there as member for the Spalding division. The noble Earl explained that the bill was one to extend the principle agreed to by the Legislators iii allowing com- pensation to labourers for their improvements.— The measure was opposed by Lord BRAMWELL, who said it would provide that no one should grant rn allotment un- less he did so under the terms of the bill —Earl FORTESCUR said he looked upon the bill as clap-trap legislation —ln supporting the bill, the Earl of DUNRAVEN remarked that if it bad not been in existence its provisions would have been included in the Government measure.—Earl Bnowettow Supported the bill, not only as a member of the Govern- ment, but as a landlord owning a large number of allot- ments —After considerable debate, Lord BRAMWELL with- drew his opposition, and the bill was read a eecond time. Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter-past seven o'clock.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THUBSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THUBSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. I IRELAND PROCLAIMED —Attention wee Celled to the recent remark of Mr. Justice Murphy to the Grand Jury of Fermanagh that nothing could exceed the peace and quiet prevailing in the county, and Mr. W. REDMOND asked on what grounds this peaceful county bad been pt °claimed.— Colonel Ktuo-fieumart replied that it wee proclaimed be- cause intimidation largely prevailed there. He further stated that the county of Westmeath had been proclaimed Mt being in a dangerous state. The county of Kildare had been proclaimed because there were 59 persons more or less boycotted. A similar inquiry as to county Down elicited the reply that it was proclaimed because some parts of it were disturbed. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—On the orders of the day being called, Mr. Slum appealed to members to assist the Go- vernment with the Irish Land Bill with as great rapidity as was consistent with the due consideration of the important matters involved. It would be difficult to carry the bill unless they passed it through committee in the earliest day of next week.—Sir W. liencounT ti ought there had not been any undue discussion of the bill.—The com- mittee then resumed the consideration of clause 4.—, Mr GRELLY moved an amendment to provide that the tenant should have power to redeem his holding in the manner provided by the Land Act of 1880 within the period of six months after service of the notice under the section, and to omit words giving power within that period to niche application for writ of restitution.—TheArromewr GENERAL for IRELAND opposed the areendment.—Sonie discussion en- eued, after which the Committee divided. For the amend- ment, 142; against, 164; majority, 22. The announce- ment of the numbers was received with Opposition cheets. MR. HEALY SUSPENDED. Mr. M. HEALY proposed to omit the second subsection of the clause, with the object of securing that the tenant after being served with a notice of eviction should still be allowed I to remain in possession of the holding until the end of the period of redemption instead of being liable to be turned out at any time. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND hoped this amend- ment would not be pressed. Mr. DILLosr said the clause would place thousands of , tenants absolutely at the mercy of the landlords. While Ithe hon. member was speaking there was some interruptions frerothe Ministerial benches, whereupon Mr. T. Healy ex- claimed, "If yoa have got anything to say, get up and Say it." (Load 'cries of "Order.") The Caeontalit : I must call on the hon. member to apol- ogise and withdraw. Mr. REALE : I have only one life to lose, and Twill lose It. While my hon. friend was speaking he was subjected to the grossest interruptions from those gentlemen. If I am to apologise, those interruptions ought to be apologised , for.

The CHAIRMAN again asked the hon. member to with- draw. Mr. T. MUM, afterconsultinc with members around him, said 4'Very well:I withdraw it." After some further discussion the Committee divided en the amendment. For the amendmmt l6O Against The CHAIRMAN' said he was under the necessity of sending for the Speaker. On the return of the Speaker, Mr. COURTNEY said Mr. De Lisle came to him to remonstrate as to his not being allowed to make an ex- planation, and Mr T Healy came to his back rind said, "Come out De Lisle if you are a man ; come out De Lisle. If you interrupt again I will break your neck." The SPEAKER aeked Mr. Healy if be had anything to say in explanation. Mr. T. klmaxy said the report of the chairman was per- fectly correct. Tbe Irish members considered interruption from the opposite side as directed against them personally, and as laving a provocative effect. He could only say that so far as he was concerned be felt no regret whatever for the course he had taken, and that he was willing to abide by the conivapence. The SPEAKER: Then I name you, Mr. Healy, to the House for having violated the order of the House. Mr. W. H. SMITH moved that Mr. Healy be suspended from the service of the Howie. .

When the motion was put the Irish members called out "No," bat Mr. T. ,Healy rose, and as he walked to- wards the door paused and said, "I beg that none of mv friends will vote against this motion; I am going out." He then left. The motion was then agreed to without opposition. The House continued sitting till a late hour.

At Wednesday's-sitting of the Wesleyan Conference a Ildepteation was received from the Nonconformist Churches Ilof Manchester. Das LANCIWOBTHY Cain : A Divriamt GRANTED.—This ease came before Mr. Justice Butt, on Tuesday. on the bus - band's application for the decree nisi to be made absolute. Mr. Bevlord, Q.C., opposed the application on basalt of Mrs Latgworthy, on several grounds—first, because about £273 for alimony remained unpaid • secondly, that there were costs not ascertained and remaining untaxed •, thirdly. on account of the £lOO a yeas interim order for the main- tenance of the child; and fourthly because of the question of appeil.—Mr. inderwick, Q.O fourth!,, the petitioner. pointed out *bat on the 6th May his client. paid £4365 into court 'in reap ct of the alimony and other matters and remarked that he was quite prepared to pay the other Charges. After some discussion Mr. Inderwick offered to pay £3,000 into court in resorct of the costs.—Mr. Justice Butt said the decree would not be made absolute until certain things hid been done by the petitioner, namely, until £273 had been paid in respect of alimony, £3OO on account of further Costs, and had said what was due in respect of the order for payment on account of the child. It was Pot within his power to withhold the decree until the question of appeal had been settled.. The decree would, therefore be made ab- solute. d ting from the day when the conditions mentioned , bed been complied with.

div.head: FRANCE.-RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.- TRADE WITH ITALY.
div.p: FRANCE.-RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.- TRADE WITH ITALY.

PARIS, MONDAY.—A railway accident occurred yester- day evening at Trappe Station, near Rambouillet. A goods train having run off the rails, blocked both the up and down lines, and in this position was run into by the 930 passenger train from Paris. Several carriages were smashed to pieces, and a number of people seriously in- jured. Another accident occurred this morning on the Western Railway near Verriers, a passenger train c"Ming into collision with a goods train. Twenty passengers were killed and several injured.

PARIS, MONDAY AVITROON.—Signori Luzotti and Elena, members of the Italian Chamber of Deputies, have arrived here to take part in the negotiations for a new commercial treaty between France and Italy. The Count de Mouy, French Ambassador at the Quirinal, will arrive to-morrow. The French Ambassadors at Berlin and St. Petersburg will arrive towards the end of the month, to consult on various matters with M. Flourens.

THE POPE *ND THE POWERS. ROY, MONDAY.—Tn a letter to Cardinal Rampolla,, published in the Moniteur de Rome to-day, the Pope speaks in terms of high compliment of England's treat- rnent of her Catholic subjects. Although reserving the question of the possession of Rome as the only practical solution of the difference Davreen_the tbiutrull and the Vatican compatible with the dignity Of the latter, Cfio tone of the document is full of conciliation, and leaves open several loopholes by which the absolute indepen- dence of the Papacy in its dealing with Christendom may be safeguarded.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.

• A shocking accident happened at St. Dunstan's Station, on the Great Northern Railway, near Bradford, on Sun- day. As two women, named Cordingley, mother and daughter, were crossing the line, the mother stumbled, and the daughter turned to her assistance, when a pas- cenger train knocked them down and killed both. A shocking accident occurred on Saturday morning on I the Chester and Birkenhead Railway, near Hooton Station. A one-legged platelayer, named Wood, very well known on the line and highly respected, was walking on the railway when he was knocked down by a special goods train travelling at a great speed, and killed instan- taneously. A loaded goods train ran away from Selling Station on the London, Chatham, and Dover Railway on Saturday afternoon, and, alter going rapidly for three miles, came into collision with fifteen trucks at Faversham with such force as to throw several trucks off the line. 'Fa elve of them were smashed up, and a guard named Stubbles, of London, who was in the runaway train, was severely crushed. his van being shattered. The injured man was removed to Canterbury Hospital. Traffic was stopped for three hours.

About 9 15 on Saturday morning, as the Hertford up train was running through the Cambridge-heath Station on the Great Eastern Railway, the driver saw a man " dive" from the platform in front of his engine. He at once applied the brake, and the train was quickly, stopped. A down main line express was approaching the station from the opposite direction, and the driver, teeing that something was wrong, also stopped his train. The passengers in 119..th.tutiv Nye% much attained at the abrtlft .iloppage of the trains, and the feeling of alarm was tollowed by one of horror as the body of the man was recovered, shockingly mutilated, from under the Hertford train.
THE DROWNING SEASON. wwned,
A bcy, named George Eddowes, was drowt on Saturday, in the river Ouse, at Stantonbury, Wolverton, while gathering water lilies.

The body of a boy named Dodd. the on of a post- master, was brought up on Monday morning in the net of a man fishing for salmon. The boy went to the river Dee to bathe on Saturday, and, getting out of his depth, was drowned.

Two shop assistants, Arthur Field, 23;'and J. IL Keep, 20, were drowaed, on Sunday, by the capsizing of a sail- ing boat near Marchwood Government powder maga- zines, opposite Southampton. Another occupant, Wm. Robinson, is in a serious state. About half-past six put., on Monday, Frederick W. Wagner, aged 15 years, after leaving his eniployment. at the Lune Works, Lancaster, went to bathe in the river with some companions. As the tide was IoW at the time, deceased said he would go further down into 'deep water. Unfortunately, he soon got out of depth, and was drowned before assistance could reach him. His body was found about 100 yards below what is known as "Barry's Hole." Deceased was a very promising lad, and his parents are Germans. Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the Imperial Hotel, Ince, on Monday, on the body of John Taylor, check weighman, who was found drowned in the canal near Rose Bridge. The deceased, who was•a collector for an insurance society in addition to his other emyloyment, bad some drink on the Wednesday. but left home on the Thursday peefectly sober. He called at an inn and had some drink, and was not seen • again until Saturday morning, when his body was pulled out of the canal. There was no watch, chain, or money. on him then, al- though he left home with - money in his possession. There was no evidence as to bow Inf.gotinto the water, and the jury returned a verdict of "Found droWned."

Another Belfast constable, Edward Keelaban, resigned on Thursday all a protest against the Crimes Act. He stated he would go 'to a free country rather than be a tool of tyranny. It is stated that an order has been received by the Trede- gar Iron and Steel Company for 280,00 sleepers for the Indian State Railway. The weight of these steel sleepers is estimated at about 9,000 tons. Articles were signed on Tuesday in the "Sporting Life" office, for a prize fight, between Jim &fifth, champion of England, End Kilraine champion of America; the fight to take place within 106 miles of Madrid,'onlanuary 3rd next. THE FRAUDS BY AN Ex-Maros.—At Chester Assizes, on Thursday, George Chapman, 74, formerly Mayor of Stockport, who had pleaded guilty to fraudulently appro- priating £11,400 he held as trust Money, was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment. ACCIDENT ON THE RAILWAY. A serious accident OC• curred about three o'clock en Thursday morning on the Manchester, Sheltie d, and Lincolnshire Railway at Ilazte- head, between Peuktone and Manchester. A waggon axle broke in a goods train from Ardwick, Manchester, to New [unkind, ihrowii,g one waggon into en adjoining field, com- pletely smashing three others, and blocking both tbe up and down lines for several hours. The night mail to Manches- ter was due five or six miautes later, but was stopped by signal.
THE Dir:-ELF.CTIONS.
BRIDGETON DIVISION OF GLASGOW.
The nomination for,the Bridgeton Division of Glasgow has been fixed for Friday, and the polling for Tuesday next.

Mr. Evelyn Ashley, the Liberal Unionist candidate for the Bridgeton Division of Glasgow, opened his election campaign on Saturday evening, by addressing a crowded meeting. He said that after studying nr George Tre- Yelyan's- speeches on Home Rule, he would ask the straightforward question from the hon, baronet whether he adhered to his statements of last year? History would praise Liberal Unionists and Conservatives for casting aside their prejudices for an object well worthy of sacrifice, and many would bless the day when the Crimes Act WM introduced, for it would not interfere with free political discussion.

div.head: SPEFCII BY Sift GEORGE TREVELYAN.
div.p: SPEFCII BY Sift GEORGE TREVELYAN.

Sir Geo. Trevelyan, Glad st on ia n can d d ate, on Monday opened his campaien in the Temperance Institute, Lan- dressy-street. He said the very existence of an organised and reorganised Liberal party in the nation WAS threatened and attacked, and he asked the Bridgeton electors whether they wished that party stamped out or wished it to be again the governing party in the State. For what was this controversy? The Liberal party, the great engine for good in the House of Commons and in the country, the historical bulwark of freedom and jus- tice, was wounded in the house of its friends. The elec- torsof Bridgeten had the opportunity of dealing a death blow at this system of pulline down the Liberal party by detail at by-elections. Did the Liberal Unionists reflect what they were doing by separating them- selves from the Liberal party?. What was the fear of every one who had read history? It was that there might be a separation of classes in the country—that all people of wealth and leisure and of rather moderate views, that so often went with wealth and leisure, should be congregated into one party, and that the Tory party. Then our politics would become what they were not now—a war of classes. And the surest way to bring that about was for a number of men of wealth, leisure, and moderate opinions, headed by Lord Hartington, to take themselves out of the Liberal ranks, and act with the Tories at elections. What good could COMP of such a course? What was the end which they proposed to themselves? If they could kill the Liberal party there would be something in it; but they could not kill the Liberal party. (Cheers.) They could not prevent it governing the country—if not now, then fire years hence—and the only result would be that they would have withdrawn from that party their guiding and restraining influence. The pre- sent election turned on three points. The first was whether the electors of Bridgeton approved lf Ireland being subjected to a bill containing unprecedented and indefensible provisions directed against free speech and free political action, and worked by a Ministry in declared sympathy with the party of ascendency in Ireland—a Ministry some members of which had actually announced that if free speech in Ireland was not put down by law it ought to he put down by violence. The second point was whether Ireland should have its opinions and aspirations defied and ignored, and its representatives treated like public enemies, or whether, on the other hand, the relations between the two islands should be arranged in a main er which would be agreeable to Leland, safe for Britain, and advantageous for both. . _ _ . _ . . . . .

(Cheers.) And the third point was whether they thought that the work of Liberalism was done and its day past— whether they were in favour of a coalition with the Conservatives and the discouragement of Liberalism by the double process of misrepresenting Liberal politicians and assisting the Primrose League to doctor and de- lude what would otherwise be Liberal constituencies, or whether they stood by the old party which had com- pelled the Tories to pass every one of the great measures to which this country owed her freedom and so much of her prosperity. He might be asked' how lie could establish that the bills of last year were dead. They were killed by the general election of 1886. The Land Pur- chase Bill was killed never to rise again, and if returned to Parliament he would resent any attempt to (same any obligatory scheme for the wholesale buying out of the Irish landlords at the risk of the British taxpayer. The other bill for the future gmernment of Ireland was dead in the body but it lived in what, was good and generous in its spirit, and lie asserted that what was good in the spirit of that bill actuated and inspired the Liberal party, and would continue to inspire it until Ireland and Britain were united not only in name but in heart. (Cheers.) Whilst he disagreed with the details of Mr. Glaclstone's bills lie used his influence inside and not out- side of the party, and he always refused to join the Liberal Unionists, describing himself not as a LiberaisUnionist but as a Liberal who had voted against the Irish bills. He always maintained a friendly tone towards his old party and its leader, and throughout the great contro- versy of last year he never used a sharp word against a brother Liberal, Mr. Gladstone was a statesman who had been famous longer than any stai esman who ever lived, and had done three times as much for the practical, and durable benefit of the nation as any legislator and administrator in her history. When, Hierefore, such a man in friendly and clear terms made an offer it should rive V' accanted & but.. lll.llloe election for North-Paddington Lord Flaitingion acted .vt. if no terms had ever been mtide by Mr. Gladstone, and urged the electors to support a Conservative candidate., It would be said that he (Sir George) left the Cabinet. He left it, not because lie had doubt about Mr. Gladstone's meaning, but because he had no doubt at all. If Mr. Gladstone had been then Willing to separate the Land Purchase Bill, to retain the Irish members, and to con- fer with him on the question of the administration of justice, as lie was now willing to confer with Lord Har- tington, he never most assuredly would have left Mr. Gladstone., People had talked about the distress of the Irish landlords till they had raised up a feeling which was only too likely to end in those landlords getting much more than their rights at the expense of the hard- working, hard-living taxpayers of this country. Thera were landlords who had had a hard, even cruel time, but as a class they were to be envied and not to be pitied by. landlords on this side of the Channel. Lord Salisbury said that if in England we had not had a fall in wheat and barley we should have heard very little about the fall of prices in Ireland. The noble lord did not know the North of England. In large, parts of Northumberland no wheat or barley was grown; and owing principally to the fall in prices, the power of the tenants to pay rent had largely fallen. The Northumberland landowners had met the case of their tenants by spontaneous reductions of rent. While he ' wished a conciliatory policy towards Ireland, whett the time came for settling the relations of Great Britain and Ireland, he should do his best to make the provisions relating to the care of law and order practical and opera- tive; and from what he had seen of leading Liberal statesmen, he did not believe that we should fail to make an arrangement which would give 'satisfaction either to British scruples or to Irish sentiments and opinions• The other point upon which there should be no mis- take was the retention of Irish .members at West- minster, and nothing would induce him to consent to their exclusion; but when tie Irish were there, lie wished they should be treated with the courtesy due to brother members. It was most discreditable that those who in., sisted on keeping the Irish members in Parliament should do so in order that, they might abuse and insult them. (Cheers.) The Irish question must remain the question of the day until it had been settled, but there were other questions. Religious equality in Wales, England, and „ Scotland was in the background, lent he cared not how . . .

soon it was in the front, tind it was well known on which side he was to be found. The House of Lords was so little representative of the opinion of the country that the Coercion Bill bad actually been passed without a division. After referring to tpiestions of loeal government, includ- ing the liquor traffie he asked the Bridgeton electors to vote for a man who protested against the fatal and irremediable policy which Lord Hartington and tldr. Chamberlain were pursuing of discouraging and breaking up the Liberal party in every constituency. Whatever the Birmingham plpers might sarabout the guiding and illuminnting influence of Lord Randolph Churchill in this new national party of which we heard 90 much, it was as dangerous as ever to render she Liberal party powerless against the day of need, and lay the country helpless and disarmed, at the disposal of Lord Salisbury and his followers. Happily the people had their fate in their own hands, and their cause annd not

be lost unless they chose to desert it themselves. Their differences were now ended, and he asked then:lp send him to Parliament as a practical and emphatic repudia- tion of the doctrine that a Liberal who voted against the bill brought in by the Liberal Government was bound thenceforward to support the Conservatives in the lobby and at the polling booths. tCheers.)

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 80, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. JULY 80, 1887.

'PRE revelation which Sir GEORGE TREV- nYA.N has felt himself compelled to make qa to the Round Table Conference, confirms What most and People have all along suspected, that People L „ , respon- sible S tuat air. t..,HAmanaPAIN is or its failure. It was pointed out by 91" Loudon correspondent that there was IjlPression amongst those who knew Mr.l O.IIAUBERLAIS best that be was going into e Conference, not with a view to bringingl ‘l,l'out the union of the Liberal party, but tattier with the object of making a show of ciltation so as to try to put Mr. GLAD- hi.°IIE in the wrong. It will be 'remembered ' repeatedly he insinuated, when the nego- ;vl4tlonB broke down, that the break-down 1.43 solely to be attributed to the leader of the eral party. The public were, for a time. Itlzzled ; they Thought it just possible Mr. I:ATONE might have declined to make any 4811Ces51on to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN; but the ktlettions or Sir W. HARCOURT and Mr. JoHtsr t,..134L5v, and, later on, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S 115"11 colleague, place it beyond a shadow of a Obt that the 'Conference failed because the %en:ll)er for West Birmingham determined it Aie°llld fail. It seems that after the first two Ittelnings there was a difficulty about getting `-. , HAIMERLAIN to a third meeting. Sir ChkGE TRETELYAN says : a, two interviews with Mr Chamberlain—On th and -ala February—duringwhich 'earnestly I re..e i ' (411'4 nted to him the very serious results that come from allowing this opportunity of re- e"lttg the Liberal party to tall through, and he t',to meet his colleagues in the conference at etiaole. I fully understood that after such a ,1 kD Itg there would be an end of asperity of lan- k •e, The dinner took place on the 14th of Feb- -Vire afterwards sat for several hours, and t, tßotiations,wlliCh had been in a very advanced 'hirereviously, were brought into a condition Ig4 left to my mind no cleat whatever that a the party was thoroughly attainable. It equent to this dinner that Mr Chamberlain L!lela 3(1 his letter in the "Baptist" newspaper, rnfer.27B.B considered by the Liberal leaders in the Ily .14ce—and, I am told, by almost all their k,„ oral‘kthe House of Commons—to be absolutely 'aci akaible with the continuance of the friendly L bic'lleiliatory negotiations which Mr Chamber- qtr. oallief had originally suggested.. %1.. rrt‘kkBERLAIN'S hostile letter resulted In trhigiPondence with Sir W. HARCOURT, iri elided in the Member for West Bir - $l4l hat he to his colleague to inform he should not rejoin the Round I e.n N `-onference. Sir GEORGE kr adds:— plv V'tr was more surprised in say life than at the plt,, wiiarned that night. Four days afterwards, eirce, r-ra Harcourt showed me the correspon- Nile e„t'aa whieo it was evident that the failure Ithnibe'tgotiatioas was due to the conduct of Mr ',I r,s`tteo,r'd'a, and that the failure was greatly re- ' th• hto the conference. When eot other parties led this result with Mr Chamberlain's per- ' 2it ~s,„uranoe to me that if I joined the confer- ' 7,r, ribi:"auld he for the purpose of renewing the Ipti; relations with our old party, I felt deeply Itiblise(Hlally and greatly pained and disappointed wefirounds. f:tobo,,a'nesday evenirg Sir W..HARCOURT ' hcENtitt'vated the statement made by Sir Gro ,thYt be_ AN. Mr. EVELYN ASHLEY "must elk len dreaming ;" for, he added, " any - Orel, Ore remote from the real history of the Os jetrillee than what Mr .A.WILEY had stated I eat ~,. Possible to conceive, and it was a , tlt'lleedtd matter of this kind should be in hqion.„ 0 serve the purpose of a contested t tr We are getting, at last, at the t,! koll'il. and nothing but the truth, as to ",, leat,nd Table Conference; and the more knit ". and r Ge ^p he more apparent it is that Sir '4EVELYAN stood alone as a Liberal
IjQ

Unionist in earnestly desiring to bring about , the union of the Liberal party. Happily, the whole of the rank and file of the party are beginning to se matters in the right light; and we trust to have further evidence of the change which is coming over men's minds at the forthcoming elections in the Bridgeton Divisim of Glasgow and in the N6rthwich Division of Cheshire. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN wrote a long letter to Mr. ASHLEY, on Thursday, giving his version of the causes of the failure of the Confer- ence. It would seem that the Liberal Unionist candidate has been floundering hopelessly; ' for Mr. CHAMBERLAIN Says :—" You are mistaken in saying th.t a letter was written to HAR COURT and MORLEY with the sanc- tion and consent of TREvELyArr." The mtmber for West Birmingham then proceeds to explain his attitude: but he finds himself so hemmed in that the only way out is to suggest that nobody but himself—not even Sir GFORGE TREVELYAN—acted throughout in good faith. He admits that Mr. Moßmtv and Sir W. HARcouRT alleged that the Conference broke down because of the offm sive letter which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN wrote to the " Baptist " newspaper ; but, he says, his view is that the "letter was a pretext and an excuse, and that the real reason for the failure of the negotiations was that in the interval between their inception and the 1.4. th February the Gladstonians had come to the conclusion that they would get their own without the necessity of yielding anything to US." Then, P.s to Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN, he adds :—" I am forced, therefore, to the ' conclusion, that his present contention is a mere afterthought, brought into the con- troversy in order to justify his extraor- dinary change of front." This sort of argument is pitiful ; it is unworthy of the man who once asnired to lead the democracy of England. There need be no wonder that his colleague in the Conference I felt "greatly pained and disappointed on public grounds." Mr. CtiAmBERLAIN has greatly pained all who looked up to him as the future Tribune of the People. He has indeed— Fallen, fallen, fallen, fallen, Fallen from his high estate.

SIR GEORGE TREVELYAN is fighting the battle of Liberalism, in Glasgow, bravely and chivalrously, and there is every reason to be I lieve that he will be returned to the House of Commons by a large majority on Tuesday next. He deserves to succeed, for, while holding tenaciously to his convictions, be has show:t that he thinks less of himself than ,of the fortunes of his party. It other Liberal Unionists had the same exalted ideas 'of duty, the split in the party would have ' long since been at an end. They are holding out against Mr. GLADSTONE, but it is difficult Ito say why they are holding out. They have even sent a Liberal Unionist, in the person of Mr. EVELYN ASHLEY, to oppose Sir GEORGE 'at Glasgow, although .they know perfectly well that at present the points of difference I between them are exceedingly small. Sir GEORGE'S sin in their eyes is that he takes ! Mr. GLA DSTONE at his word; he accepts the statement of his leader that the Irish Land Bill is dead, and that no attempt will be made to revive it in anything like the same. form ; and as to the Home Rule scheme he is contented with the assurance that Mr. GLADSTONE does not insist on excluding the , Irish members. These are points on which Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN and many other Liberals have expressed strong opinions, and, !finding that their views are not to be over- ridden, they are failing back into their places in the ranks of the Liberal party. This is the secret of the success of the Liberals at the ! recent bye-elections ; and as things go the leaders of the Liberal Unionists will ere long I find that they are leaders without followers. It is curious to note how,..since Mr. GLAD- ; STONE made his concessions. he Liberal lUnionists have collapsed so far as argument 'is concerned. Mr. EVELYN ASHLEY has i a good deal to say, but it is all summed up in trying to show that his opponent has not been consistent. But what if he succeeded in proving his t case? Would that mike the arguments in favour of Home Rule any weaker? Not in ; the least. It would simply show that Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN had not in the firs: tinstance appreciated their force, and that. like a wise man, he had changed his mind , for a good reason. And how much better lis this than the position taken up by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who calls himself a Home Ruler, and yet strives against Home Rule, I who calls himself a Liberal, and yet does all he can to break up the Liberal party I

THE Btu for making merchants and tradesmen something like honest—in the matter of Trade Marks stands on a pretty solid footinv, and has a fair chance of be- coming law. It was under consideration on Monday, at the quarterly meeting of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, and was generally approved. The measure is en- titled, "The Merchants Trade Marks Law- Consolidation and Amendment Bill," and, in its present form, it is the outcome of a compromise on two other bills on the sub- ject—one introduced by Mr. MUNDELLA, and the other by BARON DE WORMS. There can be no question that English trade has for some time suffered through the malpractices of English Traders. Goods of all kinds that are sold by length have been marked with false lengths; and, in the hardware trade, tools and cutlery .made on the Contin- ent have been sent to this country to receive an English mark, prior to being put on the market as English goods. In our own neigh- bourhood. we- have seen how the watch trade of Prescot has been brought to the verge of ruin through foreign made watches being put in English hall-marked cases, and sold as watches of English manufacture. It is ob- vious that a double injury is wrought when inferior foreign goods are palmed off with an English name. In the first place, a cer- tain amount of home labour is displaced in the manufacture of such goods. By tricks of this kind. the English workman may be left to walk the street, while his continental competitor is kept busy; and in the second place, when the goods are of poor quality— as they generally are—the reputation of English manufacturer suffers by the false mark. It rnav be said that a difficulty of , this kind should be left to right itself by the ordinary law of supply and demand—that, in the long run, those who supply an inferior article will lose custom. This is undoubtedly true, but the "long run " day be, very long, and while the grass grows the horse starves. It is told of one fraudulent tradesman, that when reminded that he would be unable to swindle a customer a second time, he an swered—" I care nothing about that; I shall be a rich man if I can swindle all the fool, in the world once only.'' It is characteristic of the togue to speak of those who trust him as fools; and it is just because Toques are so

much on the increase, and are so impudent. that an effort should be made to strike them down. It is the business of the Legislaturt• to make it easy to do right, and hard to do wrong: and it is because the Trades Marks Bill is in hirmony with this principle that we trust it will become the law of the land. Care has been taken in framing it to ensure that it shall not affect traders who err unin- tentionally, and as for the others—those who do not carry a conscience—nobody need be sorry if the new n 4 should cover them and hold them fast in its meshes.

The evening con- gregation was very good, there being a large con- tingetit from Preston Brook, the choir from the Primitive Methodist Chapel at that place kindly giving their services, and repeating some of the hymns which they recently sang at their late an- niversary. They were strengthened by Messrs. Newell and Stubbs, from Runcorn. Mr. Luke Jones led the. choir, and Mr. Charles Jones presided at the organ. Mr. James Stubbs, a Runcorn, conducted. • A WARRINGTON INFANT'S ADVENTURE.---4 few days ago some commotion was caused in the neigh- bourhood of Rnutsford-road. Warrington, conse- quent on the disappearance of a child, the son of a man named Acton, who lives at Latchford. It ap- pears that the little fellow, who is only four years old, went out to play in the morning, and as he did not return in a reasonable time, considerable un- easiness was felt by the parents, which was in- creased as night came on, and no tidings of the missing lad had been received. Inquiries were in- stituted, and it was ultimately ascertained that he was at the Golhorne police station, whither he had apparently wandered on foot. After an absence of of about twenty-four hours, he was restored to his parents. The distance from Warrington to Gol- borne is about eight miles. 'lt has also been dis- covered that the youngster stopped at an hotel at Winwick, said that he lived at Warrington, and was going home. He was gratuitously supplied with a "butty," and instead of taking the right road for i home, he seems to have wandered off n the other direction. • THE CLAIM FOR ..C5O DAMAGES.—At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before Judge Ffoulkes, an adjourned case was resumed in which Mrs Georgina Williams sued Mr. William Urquhart, draper, Newton, for .f.,50 damages for having wrong- fully deprived her of certain household furniture, for injury to the said furniture, and for money paid and incurred by reason of the defendant's wrongful action. Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Warrington, represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Swift, barrister. Liverpool, appeared on behalf of Mr. Urquhart. The circumstances on which this action was grounded have previously appealed in our columns in con- nection with an action for illegal distraint brought by the plaintiff against the defendant at Newton Petty Sessions. After witnesses had been heard on both sides Mr. Swift, for the defence, urged that the action was entirely a speculative one. He conten- ded that the goods were restored uninjured on Sat- urday the 11th, and that, as the order was only made on the 6th the detention was *very short, and not, such as to warrant damages being awarded. He also put in other minor contentions. His Honour entered a non-suit. Mr. Longton men- tioned the matter ot an appeal, and, on the applica- tion of Mr. Swift, damages were assessed by his Honour at 40s, provisionally in an appeal being made. Promptly at eleven o'clock a time drawn by four greys, was at the Pablic Offices, and the fol- lowing gentlemen took their seats :—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, H. 0,10011. juar.. R. Cook, B.
