On former pc- ' cart:one the gas works hetes been the first place visited, but this duty was dispensed with in the present instance. Under the superintendence of Mr. Cerr and the Gas Committee, with Mr. Gaekell at their head, the works are in a most efficient condition and as there was no new process in opera- tion to interest the members, it was deemed unneceisary to Inspect the works. The party were therefore at once driven 'through Lngsdale to the Infectious Diseasee Hospital. The building, which is fist approaching completion, stands on three acres of land, off Crowwood-line, near Halton View, purchased at a coat of £BOO from the trust of the Leigh estate, and is distant about otto and a bait miles from the centre of the township. There are four wards, two intended to rec.tive three beds each, and two calculated to bold two beds each. This accommodation is that fixed by the Local Government Board, but upon an emergency double the number of beds could be introduced into the building. The rooms are heated by open fire places, and Boyle's patent ventilators are fixed in the walls and also und.r the beds. A striking feature of the outside of the structure is a verandah run- ning nearly the whole length of two sides of the building. . and its eurpoee is to allow the patient.) to have Ft little fres?, air during the early period of convalescence.. Colonel Roth. well, of St. Helens, is the contractor for the wet it, and Mr. JartWA Sadler is clerk of works. Below the boepital on the easterly side there is also now in ceurse of construction a caretaker'e cottage, comptising a medical officyea room, a ki.chen, ecul len, and mantra, three bedrooms, and an attic. The total clef, including the ale, will be about £3,400: Tee members of the Beard made a tboroaAh , examination of the structure, and appeared to • ba highly Satisfied with the work and the arrantremente. The party was then driven to Pex Hill, where the covered reservoirs are situated, and found everything in "apple-nie order." It is gratifying to notice that during an unprecedented seeeon of drought there has not been the slightest scarcity of water, and al. the time of the visit there was upwards of lel feet of watrr iin the reservoirs. A light lunch having been pertaken or, the horses' heads were turned towards Socks Well, which has been the scene of some remarkable engineering opera.. lions dutine the past twelve months. In the early part al 1 1886 the demand for water had increased at such an enor- mous rate as to be within about 10 per cent. of tee available simply, and to prevent the possibility of anything in aid shame of a water famine arising the Gas and Water Com- mittee At once instituted an inquiry as to the beet means t 1 increasing the supply. The quantity of water at tiris tin 3 beieg used for domestic purposes, although less Lb at ia ttrj majority of towns, was considered much too great, and the ' first step of the committee was the introduction of Deaconie patent waste water meters for the deection and pleventiert of ondergri nod leakages and unnecessary waste. Thrl work being in progress the committee next directed their attention to Stocks well,the old pumping station of the Board, I where the yield had for come time par been eraduatly failing. The decrease in five years amounted to about one fourte ef ' previous total. It wag, bee evee, patent to all that an aban- . ' (feet supply of water c mid be obtained provided the pumpe . were fixed eta lower level. The questi tn of how le.st 'Ca , accemelish this was for a Vele a vexed ontl. To sink the wen deeper and lower the old pumps was the first idea, bur, finally this was abandoned on the grounds of its being moat expensive and with substrata such as is to be mel.. with at Stocks Well, not always a reliable course, and a' scheme recommended be the Beard's engineer, Mr. Caere was sdepted for lowering a set of pumps late the existing. 241 n. hire hole, which extends to a depth of 250 feet baba ' tha bottom of the well. The Increased quantity of water semred by this eche me, say 300 millions per annum, wilt , meet the pres•nt rate of increase, Which is I about 11 per cent, for from three to four year!. At the time of the Visit the engine was beautifully clean and bright, and the whole of the ponderous and compli- . cated machinery was wtrking with remarkable smother is. , Me. Carr exhibited to the members simples of water !akru during the past five days, during which period tbe ere:in° bad been at work. In the first sample there wae a twderate sediment of mineral substances, but in the last the as ales was as clear as crystal, and there wee no perceptible dere sit. Netherly Pumping Station was next visited. The buildirgs and machinery were in the best of cendition, and after ta cursory glance round, the members went te visit the book, about which so much has been said and written during the plat three years. It is no exeggearation to say that the brook was in a most filthy state, and the effluvia that arose therefrom was intensely disagreeable Following the stream above the Bridge, the party stw whe-e the brook, divided into two streams up to that noint, became one watercourse. One stream drains the neighbourhood of Huyton, Roby, atc and also receives the water from the sewage farm belonging to those townships. The other ft ma past Gateacre, dec. It was a striking fact that, although the water in the latter breech was clear and Pellucid, the firmer was of a naio elete colour, and gave eff a most offensive odour. Wo fur- ther demonstration of the source of the pollution was needed, sod several of the gentlemen present rp ire in strong terms upon the matter. We understand, however, that an injunction has been obtained to restrain the Heyton and Roby Local Board from turning the overflow of tbe seeige farm into the brook at a point beyond the residence of Mr Jump, who has taken a prominent part in the attempts to prevent the nuisance. When this is done it is hoped that. all reason for complaint will disappear. and it may be stated for the satisfaction of the ratepayers that the Widnee Local Board are fully alive to the importance of Leepinet the gathering ground of the pumping stations free from pollution, and a very watchful eye will ha kept. upon any. thing having a tendency to injure the present abundant atct , pure supply of water. Upon leaving Netherly the party were driven ti Hemel Crees Hotel, where they sat down to a repast served in t most satisfactory fashion by Mr. flilditcb, the landlord. .A a heavy and continuous downpour of rain succeeded, . most of the gentlemen returned home by train.

The election at Newton has resulted in the return of the three retiring Commissioners : but the contest has done good inasmuch as it has brought the Commissioners face to face with their constituents. There has been some plain speaking on both sides ; and plain speaking in the present is likely to prevent misunderstanding in the future.

It is stated that Lord Char!es Beresford has tendered his resignation because, at the Naval Review, he signalled a private message to his wife from a Royal yacht, thereby being guilty of a breach of etiquette. It is hardly likely that the Queen will accept his resigna- tion. 1 he had signalled to another man's wife, it might Lcve, gone hard with him.

William Moody, the young and " enter- prising burglar," who kept a yacht, and did business at Toulton-cum-Seacombe in the early hours of the morning of the zoth May, has had a stop put to- his remantic career. He has been sentenced to five years' penal servitude. and, for some lime to come, it is not unlikely that he will be more Moody than ever.

Alderman Burgess seems to , have been misunderstood in saying to an aged ne'er-do- weel the other week— You are getting near the end?' " The end" has been taken to mean the end of the woman's life, whereas Alderman Burgess meant the end of her mendicancy. An explanation having been made, the Home Secretary sees no reas)n to interpose in the matter.

Mr. Grain, the solicitor who acted for Miss Cass. seems to have given offence to the court officials by his searching cross•examina- don ef Madame Pietra. But it was his duty to show. if he could, that she was not a trust- worthy witness. Character is everything in an inquiry whete character is so much al •;tal:e. It is gratifying to see that Miss Cass has stood the ordeal wonderfully well.
The following neat parody of a celebrated epigram is from "Tar h ": THE THREE WILLIAMS. (Gladstone, Harcourt, and Smith.)

Three Williams, to three different stations born, The British House of Commons now adorn; The first holds place unrivalled in debate, The next deals blows that heavy are and straight; The third, unable to such lines pursue, The closure puts, and gags the other two.

The Tories, after ridiculing what was called the "three acres and a cow" pro- posal, are utilising the idea by bringing in a bill upon the subject. The Government feel that they owe Mr. Jesse Collings something for his support, and this is how they are paying him. It is very poor pay, it must be confessed, for the bill does not give " three acres and a cow ; " the maximum allotment is one acre, and there is nothing said about the cow.

The Bill has what are called compulsory powers; but it is a farce to call them com- pulsory. The labourer who wants an allot ment has to apply in the first instance to the landowner; failing here, he is to apply to the sanitary authority, who are to petition the county authoiities, who in their turn have to go to Parliament for a bill confirming a provisional order. He will be a very clever labourer who puts all this machinery in mo- tion. It is not too much to say that, if the bill pass as it stands, it will be as great a failure as the A.rtizans Dwellings Act framed by Lord Cross.

Speaking at Norwich, on Wednesday night. Lord Salisbury referred to the " affection" which he and his friends had for Ireland. affection That is about the coolest thing one •has heard of this hot weather.; it is as refreshing as the rain. You proclaim the whole of Ireland.; you put the Irishman in a straight jacket, and then you ask him to accept it as a proof of your "affection:"

Lord Salisbury's impudence was not ,con- fined to his reference to Ireland. He spoke of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill as being "as dead as all the skeletons of abandoned con- victions and deserted causes with which the path of his life is strewn.'•' Lord Salisbury cannot 'forgive Mc. Gladstone for having grown out of the .",small clothes" of the Tory party; but since he has done so his name has been "writ large" on every page of the statute book that contains something of benefit to the ,peopie of this country. And what of the Prime Minister? Bah! It is sufficient to say that he stands before the world -a convicted "-Salisbury."

At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a poor wrwnan was fined five shillings for neglecting to send her boy to school. She pleaded that the School Attendance Officer came in the house "more like a big dog," that the boy had had a sore throat, and that the Schoolmaster said he would not have him at school because it was " catching." But :t was no use pleading ; the Ene had to be paid. When education becomes free, there will be an end to these petty prosecutions at petty sessions.

- - Mr. John Morley subjected ,the Govern- ment to a merciless criticism on Saturday. After quoting Lord Salisbury' g views on the question of revising rents, and showing how he had eaten his own words. he added :'— "So you have got in April Lord Salisbury rejecting the policy which in May he accepts You have got him in June again rejecting the policy which he had accepted in May, and you have him in July accepting the policy which he had rejected in June." They say he who cannot turn cannot spin. Lord Salis- bury ought to be a good spinner.

Lord Salisbury does not appear to be in favour of arbitration. In the House of Lords, on Monday, Lord Bristol moved "That this House, in view of the yearly increasing ar- maments of European nations, is of opinion that the formation of an international tri bunal for the reference of national disputes, in the first instance, is highly to be desired.' Lord Salisbury threw cold water on the motion, urging that there was no probability of the formation of a tribunal for dealing with national diFputes. Of course not, nor will there be until some nation takes the lead. Public opinion wants educating, and the way to educate it is to pass such a resolution aF, Lord Bristol proposed.

NOTES BY THE WAY.
On Saturday the game between Lancashire and Glouces- tershire was brought to an early conclusion, Lancashire being left the victors by an innings and 98' runs. . . _

With nine wickets to fall and 302 runs wanted to save a single inning's defeat, the Sussex men had a hopeless task before•them at Brighton on Saturday morning, but though the wicket was dusty and rather difficult, especially at one end, they ought certainly to have made a better score than they did. They only added 73 to their overnight total of 14. and were all out in two hours, Notts winning the match by an innings and 289 runs—a most decisive victory. On Wednesday, alter a varied day's cricket, Yorkshire managed to gain a well-deserved victory over Gloucester- shire by 70 runs. At the drawing of the stumps on Tues- day, an innings had been completed on each side and York- shire had lost one wicket in their second innings for 65. the hone county being 36 runs on with nine wickets to fail Had the wicket remained good there is little doubt that the match would have been drawn, bat rain fell heavily during the greater part of Tuesday night and completely altered the aspect of the game. In the match at Kennins ton Oval, on Monday, the Leicesterehire wickets went down rapidly at the hands of the Surrey men, who dismissed their opponents in an hon.. and a half for 57. The first five batsmen were out for 15 runs.

The paragraph is headed "A Brutal Magistrate."
HORRIBLE MURDER IN SHEFFIELD:

'A shocking murder was committed on Saturday at Sheffield, preceded by an attempt to murder a servant 071. The scene of the murder is a house occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Stothardt. Shortly before eleven a.m., a man named Hobson went to the house, and asked for some water. Soon afterwards he returned with another request, and then, during the temporary absence of Mrs. Stothardt he endeavoured to cut the servant girl's throat. On Mrs. Stothardt' s return he cut her throat, severing the jugular vein. Death must have been almost instantaneous. The girl rushed out into the street, and her cries soon briught, some of the neighbours on the scene. Hobson got away whilst some of them were actually within a few yards of the house. Early in the afternoon he was apprehended close to one of the railway stations. . - .

At the Sheffield Police Court, on Monday, Henry Hobson. was brought up charged with having niurdered Mrs. Ada Stothardt on Saturday, and with hating attempted to murder a servant girl named Florence Mosley. On• the application of the Chief Constable he was remanded; pending the holding of an inquest. The prisoner did not seem to feel his position, and he has ever since his arrest shown the utmost coolness. Some hours after his apprehension the police • discovered that there were marks of blood on his- trousers and similar stains on his coat. In each case they were recent. The knife with which the murder was committed has not been found. Hobson has been identi- fied amongst a number of prisoners as the man who was seen leaving the deceased woman's house just before the murder was discovered, and who said " They are making a mess in there, he's gone upstairs." No motive for the murder can be ascertained except that Hobson believes he lost a situation through the deceased . woman's husband.

div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. Chamberlain, in acknowledging a resolution on the Irish Land Bill, passed by the Edinburgh Liberal Unionist Association, writes;—" I have received with much gratification the resolution accompanying the letter. lam glad to say that there is every prospect that the Government will meet with the wishes of the Liberal Unionists with regard to the Land Bill, by reasonable and satisfactory concession."

Mr. Goshen writes, through his secretary, that, owing to engagements, he cannot address the Glasgow St. Rollox Liberal Unionists. Had it been possible he would have been glad to have assistect the Unionist cause in Glasgow, where such good work has been done by the Liberal Unionists, the progress throughout Glasgow and the West of Scotland generally being a hopeful augury and welcome encouragement to Unionists in every part of the United Kingdom. Mr. Cunningham 'Graham, M.P., wrote to the Glas- gow Mail, on Saturday, in reference to an article on Lord Hartington's capabilities, in the Edinburgh Review, in which be says he cannot say that though a cow once walked upstairs, and said "I triumph," the Liberal party should have such a bovine leader as Lord Harting- ton. The man is honest, but intensely stupit, and swarms in Midland counties in smock frocks. We have a leader in Mr. Gladstone, and a successor in Mr. Morley. A memori d signed by a large number of members on both sides of the House of Commons was last week for- warded to Mr. Smith asking him to fix a morning sitting a Tuesday, and give The evening sitting for the dis- cussion of ir Wilfrid Lawson's resolution in favour of giving local communities a legal power of restraining the issue or renewal of liquor licenses. Mr. Smith in- formed Sir Wilfrid at the close of Friday's sitting that he was sorry the business of the House was in such a state tbat.he could not at present comply with the request. PROTEST OF PEERS AGAINST THE COERCION ACT. . _
The following protest against the Coercion Bill, signed by Liberal peers, has been placed on the journal of the House of Lords:— _

Dissentient: (I) Because exceptional criminal legisla- tion weakens the ordinary administration of justice, by inducing reliance on arbitrary methods, and is at the ' best only temporary in its effect, while it causes lasting irritation and intense hatred and mistrust of law. (2) Because, while it is the fact that in some parts of Ireland the people do not support the administration of the law, we do not, after nearly two years' freedom from excep- tional legislation, see evidence of such an amount of crime and lawlessness at the present time as has been held to justify Parliament in enacting measures of special severity. (3) Because this bill gives the Irish Executive a power on its own responsibility to deprive the whole or any part of the Irish people of those consti- tutional safeguards and individual rights which are so justly prized in Great Britain. (4) Because, even if some change in the law of criminal procedure in Ireland be ex- pedient, it is not right to submit for judicial determina- tion questions most difficult of solution, such as charges of conspiracy, to subordinate tribunals dependent upon the will of the Executive. (5) Because this bill is not only directed against crime and outrage, but against as- sociations lawful in their • objects and methods, which are placed at the mercy of the Executive, *he,never such associations in the opinion of the Executive disturb the tnainte,nance of law and order. (6) Because such legislation is likely to create and stimulate the action of secret societies, which will be more dangerous than open associations. (7) Because thc experience of a long series of repressive acts conclusively show that excep- tional legislation of the kind has failed to secure any permanent respect for law and order, while it tends to render the present system of government in Ireland odious to Irish people. (8) Because the only true remedy for the evils which this this bill is intended to meet is to be found in legislation which will bring the people of Ireland into harmony and sympathy with the law and its administration. The protest is signed by the 'following peers :—Gran- ville, Spencer, Ripon, Kitnberley, Wolverton, Braye, Rosebery, Sandhurst, Ilerschell, Orinbridge, Hamilton of Dalzell, Houghton, Northbourne, Hampden, Seton, Kensington; Leigh, Hot hfield, Burton, Camoys, Hobhouse, Monkswell. Sydney, Thring, Chesterfield, and Greville. The ROuND Timm CONrmtwsCE.—Mr. Chamberlain has written a letter to the Hon. Evelyn Ashley, the Liberal Unionist condidate for the Bridgeton Division of Glasgow, in which be criticises Sir George Trevelvan's statements about the Bound Table Conference. He contends that air George has absolutely and uncenditionaily surrendered the main point for which he sacrificed bin position in the Cabinet and his seat in the House of Commons. Tice Liseeer, UNIONISTS.—The Liberal Unionists held their first annual general meeting on Wednesday, at Willis's Rooms, London, when it was stated that the financial posi- tion of the union was eminently eatisfactory. Sir H. James, who presided, contended that every Gladstonian who had met with success at recent by-elections had practic illy ac- knowledged the justice of the leading objetions of the Liberal Unionists to Mr. Gladstone'd Horne Rule Bill of last year, and Mr. Chamberlain expressed confidence in the future prospects of the Union.

LORD Sentsnuns AT NORWICR.—On Wednesday night, the Marquis of Salisbury addressed a large meeting of Eastern Counties Conservatives and Unionists in the Agri- cultural Hall at Norwich. Speaking of the foreign policy of the Government, the Prime Minister said he now saw Egypt in a state of repose. The country was settling down slowly in the paths of civilised government, and the entire drift ef the policy would be waved if they conceived that the wliole of it depended upon whether the Convention was ratified or not. The Convention was principally useful to Turkey, and we should suffer nothing by its rejection. What we had gained was two years of gradual pacification, which had removed for many years the terrible state of things which existed in 1885, and for this and many other reasons the negotiations had been, in his judgment, of the greatest value. Be said the same with regard to the Afghsn negotiations. Referrirg to domestic legislation, he said the obatructionists were resolved that the wheels ef Parliament should not turn round. The noble Marquis then proceeded to criticise the policy of Mr. Gladstone on the question of Home Saile.-0a Thursday Lord Salisbury was entertained at luncheon by the May u. of Norwich, and afterwards received addresses from 120 Conservative asso- ciations, representing the eastern counties. In the course of his reply, his lordship said his political experience confirmed that of the old French statesman who said that the unforeseen always happened. They should, therefore. he always prepared for a possible election.

MR JOHN MORLEY ON THE IRISH POLICY OF THE GO- VERNMENT —On Saturday Mr. John Morley opened the Hackney Reform Club, and in the course of his speech attacked the palicy of the Government w,ith regard to Ire- land. Alluding to Lord Salisbury's vacillation on the question at revising rents, he said his lordship now accepted the policy of revision in a much wider form than he had rejected it a month ago. What the Chief Secretary said would los madness and folly in March was tccepted as the fast words of wisdom and of statesmanship in July. Then the position of the Chancellor of the Exchequer shocked him immensaly. He had been striving harder than anyone to pass the Coercion Bill, and now he bad practically ac- cepted and enforced upon Parliament Mr. Parnell's own policy, and told Mr. Parnell in very courteous language that he was very glad that he had been fortunate enOUgh to get his approval. He (Mr. Morley) was sure the Dissentient Liberals were deluding themselvss if they thought that the proposals which were dependent upon the passing of a Tory measure of land purchase were only temporary proposals. The Government mizbt vacillate and waver, but Liberals would not be content with any setl,ment of the Irish ques- tion which did not give to Irish:l.:en a full and effictiye coo- trot over al affairs and matters which Parliament should declare to be Irish alLirF..

div.head: SHOCKING ]MATH OF MR. GEORGE
div.p: SHOCKING ]MATH OF MR. GEORGE
MACKEY.

On Wednesday morning Mr. George Mackey, who was until a few months ago master at Warrington Workhouse, met with a shocking death at the Cen- tral Station, Warrington. Since April Mr. Mackey has been engaged as cashier by Mr. Robert Beaton, contractor, and it was while on his way to Mr. Heaton's offices adjoining the Central Station a little before eight o'clock that he received the injuries from which he died. Mr. Mackey lived at School-brow and, it appears, that the nearest way from his home to Mr. Heaton's office was along the line and through the goods yard.. Mr. Mackey had been in the habit of taking this route, and on Wednesday morning he was going through the goods yard when he was knocked down by a wag- gon that was being shunted and terribly injured by two of the wheels that passed over him. The acci- dent was witnessed by some of the railway servants, and &stretcher was procured and the injured man was speedily conveyed to the Infirmary. Mr. Heaton having been informed of the sad event, had previously taken a cab, and hurried to the Infirm- ary, so that Dr. Richmond was at once in attend- ance on the arrival of Mr. Mackey. It was soon seen, however, that there was little hope of re- covery, and death ensued about an hour after ad- mission to the Infirmary. Mrs Mackey, accom- panied by Mrs Heaton, reached thelnfirmairy just before her husband breathed his last. Mr. Mackey was 54 years of age, and leaves a widow and six children. Mr. Mackey was appointed to the post of master of the Warrington ,Workhouse in 1869, and had previously held a similar office for five years at the Lisnarick Workhouse, County Ferma- nagh, Ireland. He resigned his position as master of the Warrington Workhouse in March last, under circumstances which will, no doubt, be familiar to most of our readers. Apart from his official capa- city, he did not, during his lengthened stay in War- rington, take any active part in connection with public matters, but he was well known and res- pected in the district. He was a member of the local lodge of Freemasons. THE INQUEST. On Thursday afternoon an inquest was held as to the death of l•fr. Mackey, by the county coroner, Mr. Brighouse, at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-st., Warrington. Mr. F. Simpson was present on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Committee, and Mr. R. Heaton was also present. Mr. Robert Heaton was the first Witness called. He said: I am a contractor and carting agent, liv- ing at Warrington. Deceased was formerly work- house master, but at the time of his death he was in my employ as cashier. He had been in my em- ploy since April. Deceased was 54 years of age. I last saw him alive at eight o'clock on Tuesday evening. I first saw him on Wednesday morning, after he had received•the injuries, a boy having come down and told me about five minutes to eight o'clock. The accident had occurred about five mi- nutes before. I went to the top of the goods yard, and saw the deceased was being put on a stretcher. I told the people there to bring him on to the Infir- mary to which place I drove in a cab, got the doctor up, and got everything ready for Mr. Mackey's arrival. On being brought to the Infirmary, deceased was placed on a bed; and he seemed to recognise me as he raised his hand, and this I understood to mean that Mrs. Mackey should be sent for. I did not know at that time what his injuries were, but the doctor said, "I believe he will die, Heaton." I after- wards sent for Mrs. Mackey, and she went to the Infirmary. I did not again see Mr. Mackey alive. Mr. Mackey lived at School-brow, and if he came down the line from the back of his house it was about half the distance by any other way. Since he has been with me he has been in the habit of com- ing that way. He had no right there, but being connected with me the railway servants did not in- terfere, because his duties sometimes took him there. The place where the accident took place is the siding part of the goods yard. Deceased was a bit deaf.

William Ashton said: lam a shunter in the em- ploy of the Cheshire Lines Railway Company. I knew the deceased by sight, and I knew he was in the employ of Mr Heaton. On Wednesday morning deceased passed me in the goods yard, and after he got about 50 yards away I was sending a waggon over the front road. I saw him in the act of cross- ing the metals when the buffer of the waggon caught him and knocked him on to tho metals. The wheels of one aide of the waggon went over him. At the time the waggen was started deceased was walking about 100 yards away close to the metals, and when I saw him I shouted" Look up" as hard as I could, but he took no notice. By Inspector Spinks-: At the time I unhooked the waggon from the engine deceased had his back towards me, and did not see me unhook it. There was a very. strong wind blowing at the time. By the Coroner: The waggon knocked him face downwards. At the time I first saw him he was not in such a position as to make it necessary for me to warn him.

Peter Clayton said : I am a goods guard in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Railway Cdmpany. I first saw Mr. Mackey on Wednesday morning about twelves or fifteen yards from where he was knocked down. He was walking about four or five yards from the outside rails butthe next time I saw him he had his leg over the rail, stepping into the four-foot, when the waggon was only a yard and a ,half or two yards from him. I shouted to him and ,he turned his head to the wagon. At the time he was making for the line the waggon must have been making towards him. The waggon would make some noise but not much. ! By Mr. Simpson: Deceased could have gone all the way down to the office without crossing the line from where I first saw kim. By Inspector Spinks : If he had occasion to go to

div.head: NAVAL REVIEW BY THE QUEEN.
div.p: NAVAL REVIEW BY THE QUEEN.

. As the morning of Saturday, slowly broke ever the Solent, there was a clear and almost cloudless sky, which would have been creditable if the scene had been laid in southern Italy instead of in the notoriously treacherous latitudes of the British Isles. A light north- westerly breeze gradually cleared away the slight haze which hung over the vast fleet quietly reposing at anchor off Spithead, and as the sun rose and lighted up the waters, glancing off the well-kept sides of the ships, the scene assumed a grandeur, and withal a fascinating beauty. From an early hour numerous craft were astir among the lines of still quiescent warships, threading their way with even motion over the placid surface of the scarcely ruffled Solent. As the morning wore on, the bustle and activity which were about to characterise the day began to be apparent on the decks of the vessels, already ranged in review order from east to west as far as the eye could reach. At eight o'hlock, as if by magic, every vessel in view became simultaneously d'ecorated with a radiant displayed bunt- ing, which fluttered in the morning breeze as it was quickly run aloft., until the whole fleet appeared like one vast and serried' series of miniature rainbows. At this moment, too, there thundered forth from the portholes of the venerable old liner, the Duke of Wellington, a royal salute to the standards of the Prince of Wales and the King of Greece, which floated side by side from the Royal yacht Osborne, as she lay at a buoy off the Royal Jetty. By and by the approaches to the Dockyard be- came filled with a steadily flowing stream of carriages laden with passengers in possession of tickets for one or other of the troopships detailed to convey visitors through the line of the war vessels. The arrangements for diverting this stream of traffic through the various roads of the Dockyard to the various ships were adrnieable. On entering' the gates conspicuous signboards pointed the way to the jetties alongside which lay in double and sometimes treble tiers the not inconsiderable fleet of troopships and smaller Government craft upon which fell the duty of carrying the thousands of sightseers who had for several days been flocking into Portsmouth and its immediate neigh- bourhood. Besides the throngs of temporary or perma- nent residents, there rolled into the yard quite an army of visitors, bah official and private, brought by special trains mainly from London, and as vessel after vessel cleared the mouth of the harbour and proceeded on its route through the lines, the excite- ment among the dense crowds which had assembled on every available space on the piers, beach, and sea walls increased. This was maintained at a high pitch throughout the efternoon, culminating about four o'clock, when the opening guns of a salute, which was rapidly taken up by the ships until it became general throughout the fleet, announced that the Queen had left Cowes. A few minutes later and the ships taking part in the Royal processions hove in sight, and steamed slowly and majestically along the course indicated in a chart. As the Royal' yacht approached each vessel manned yards, or, in the case of the turret ship, the men were arranged around the ship and her turrets, and round after round of British cheering paned along the lines, raising a feeling of genuine enthusiasm such 0 could hardly have been equalled under any other cir- ciimstances. Moored off the Rs-de Sand and over the Motherbank were some score ef magnificent merchant' vessels, representing all the largest shipping companies of the kingdom, and a dense fleet of yachts. These vessels, like the men-o'-war, were profusely de- corated with bunting, forming an unrivalled display in thgmselves, and the shouts of loyalty and welcoffie which burst forth in peals from them added greatly to the effect of The more regular cheering by word ef command from the warships. The beach of Stokes Bay, particularly around the Gilkicker Point and Fort, was densely packed with people, and the enthu- siasm of the moment spread to them also, the oft-re- newed bursts of cheering only dying away when the leading vessels of the Royal procession reached tile easternnerst end of the columns. , In certain of the vessels which followed in the procession the visiters had mounted to the tops, and some few even to the cross- trees, and the unusual spectacle of grave and even aged senators, fashionably ttired, swarming aloft in silk or tall gray hats was not a little droll to the nautical eye. Her Majesty was accompanied on her tour by the Lords of the Admiralty and her naval au/es-de-came, and she continually expressed her admiration and the plea- sure which the review was affording her. At its close she caused the following signal to be given, throtieh the Lords of the Admiralty.' to Admiral Sir Georges Willes' the Commander-in-Chief, whose flag was living aboard the Inflexible—" Her Majesty has great satisfaction arid pride at the magnificent display by her navy this after- noon." After completing a, lengthened tour of the fleet of British ships of war, her Majesty approached those of foreign nations, which lay at anchor off Bresendown. One Dutch vessel, two French training ships, and a Ger- man vessel had taken part in the dressing, 811 W-saluting, and cheering simultaneously with the English vessels„ As the Royal yacht left the British fleet the thunders of salute pealed forth a parting greetipg; end the nayal review of 1887, so long an absorbing tome, was over. • During the salute on board the gunboat Kite, .a charge was placed in, the gun either before the latter had been pronerly sponged or before the breech had been closed. The result was a premature explosion of the cartridge, by which four men were iniurecl. It was sub- sequently reported that one man had died from the in- juries he received. That no collision occurred where the waters were so alive with craft of every description, speaks well for the organised arrangements, and for 'the, skill and care displayed by officers entrusted with the navigation of the vessels which throughout the whole day were continually passing between Spithead and Portsmouth harbour. . . . _

Late on Sunday night a service dingey was capsized, and a leading at,..lcer named Moore, belonging to 44 Tor- pedo boat, was drowned. Three other men .were rescued in .a very exhausted condition, but are progressing, favourably.

The clerk to tbe Abergele magistrates attributed the refnaal to pay tithe to the agitation going on in the Radical press, and to the teaching of Mr. Devitt and his friends.

THE BOLTON STreiss.—The strike at Baton has now entered upon its eleventh week. Hopes are still entertained that the dispute may be referred to arbitration. On Sunday the county policemen visited All Saints' Church, and in th, afternoon a Bolton clergyman who had intended to preach to the imported men at Messrs. Dobson and Barlow's works was locked in a class..room by a number of his scholars, and informed that if he visited the works hie csuroh and schools would be boycotted. The "knobsticks" had no minister. The Bolton magistrates. on Thursday morning. ordered Mary Macdonald, Ann Owen, and Margaret Bankm to find sureties for three months, and James Gradwell and John Lnmax for six months, or in default one month's im- prisoner nt, for creating a disturbance in connection with the local strika. The Warrington Tbiat Iron at,d Brno Wiredrawers' Society havo ro-nitted through the War- rington United Trades Council £2 in akl of the Boltea en- gineers.

div.head: WABIIINGTON SAILING CLUB.
div.p: WABIIINGTON SAILING CLUB.

The second annual match of the Warrington Sailing Club took place on Saturday. Additional interest was given to the contest by the presence of two new boats, viz., the Oriana, which is not the Oriana of last year, but a new 25ft. cutter-rigged boat, introduced by Mr. Bedell, the wmroodore of the club, and the siesta, a 21ft. centre board, which has been recently built at Warrington by the owners. Messrs. T. and W. Jackson, and was making her first trip dawn the river. Another feature of interest was the re-appearance of the Gipsy, an old Warrington favourite, which has returned after a long absence to her original moorings. The follow- ing boats sailed in the race, and we give also their owner's names, the club measurement, and the time allowance of each respectively, in minutes : —Gipsy (J. Whitfield), 51ft. 10in., scratch; Grimm (G. P. Bedell), 45ft,, Bin„ 6min. ; Siesta (T. and W. Jackson), 42ft. 3in. 9min.";!Maggie (F. W' Monks), 38ft., 14 min.; Clara (R. 'Jefferson), 33ft.. • 10in., 18min. ; Comet (M. Nosworthy), 28ft. 6in, 23imin. The presence of five other sailing boats and four steam launches under weight in Bank Quay reach at the same time Erave the river an 'unwonted- ly gay appearance. Tim course sailed was from Atherton's Quay to the Clarence training ship, off New Ferry, and the start was made shortly after high water, on a rapidly falling tide, and with but a light breeze from the north6west. After 'the long drought, there was naturally very little water in the channel, and all the boats, suffered more or less delay thron.:h getting aground All succeeded in getting off again, and as the wind; although at one tiine • scarcely perceptible, did not fail altogether, the whoie of the boats sailed thoit<course, the last round- ing the Clarence just before the tide . turned. The Orialia having, through some mismanagement at the start got away with a considerable lead, lost ground a little in the narrow channels above Runcorn, and touched bottom in Seeking to discover a new deep o through the Che- shire arch, but afterwards more than regained her position, coming in 104 minutes before the next boat. The next four boats started together, and the Maggie led for some distance, but got aground below the Ferry and lost her advantage,the two passing Runcorn Bridge together, and maintaining the same positions until Rale was reached,where the Siesta drew ahead and took the second place. The Gipsy having grounded in the Ferry reach. and again below the Round Cheyerel, on one occasion breaking her keel- chain, passed Runcomfouraninutes after the Siesta and Maggie, but in the more open .water she gained ground, and came in third, the time ailowance,how- ever, setting her ha& to the fourth place. The plucky little Comet came in next, and,with the help of her large time allowance, only,two minutes later, and some 20'minutes before the Clara.. On compar- ing the well-formed and well-sailed little fleet which took part in the match with the style of boat with which we used to be familiar, the club may reasonably congratulate itself on having done something to improve the position of 'boating on the Upper Mersey, as well as to provide amusement for its members.

div.head: CLAIM AGArNsr A NEWSPAPER
div.p: CLAIM AGArNsr A NEWSPAPER

• PROPRIETOR. At Warringten County Court, on Thirrsday,bafore his Honour Jinige Flounces, a case was heard in which Ernest Jones, journalist, of 17iGordon-street, Islington, London, sued,Paul Hall, of Earlestown, ' the proprietor of the " Earlestown Genirdian," on a claim for £32, alleged to be due by defendant in lieu of three months notice .to terminate an engage- ment entered into between himself and the plain- tiff. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor. Warrington, appeared , for the plaintiff, and Mr. Harper, solicitor, Man'- chester, for,the defendant. Mr. Jenkins,4 in detail- ' ing particulars of the:plaintifrs claim,. said it ap- peared that in the early part of this year plaintiff inserted an advertisement in the' "Daily NeWs," which was answered by the defendant, and a. correspondence 'ensued. Defendant ul- timately accepted the services of the plaintiff. ' The agreement which settled the terms of the en- gagement was made on the 15th of March, 1887, and set forth that Paul Hall was the preprietor of the "Earlestown Guardian," a weekly newspaper, and that the plaintiff had agreed to u,ndertake the managing editorship and other work of the said newspaper. Tire plaintiff, the engagement said, was to be managing editor, reporter, ,canvasser, Sz.c, of the newspaper, ,to ;write articles and notes, col- lect accounts, read proofs, keep books, and do what the said Paul Hall might deem necessary to pro- mote his interests.. Plaintiff was to receive 50s per week, and a commission of 15 per cent for all nd- vertisement& obtnined by him by personal canvas,l provided that he obtained no less than .no worth of advertisements within the first three months of the engagement The engagement was to be. for three months certain, and after the, expiration the engagement to. he terminable on any day in the year, by either party giving to the other three calendar months notice in writing. Having read the agreement, Mr. Jenkins said that the plaintiff entered upon his duties in Hades- town by going, there on the 4tb April, but, as a matter of fact, he commenced performing certain work c nected with the newspaper on the let April. Before leav- ing London he did certain ivork by canvassing for adver- tisements, and he also wrote a leading article which he forwarded to the defendant. /go objection was made as to his not commencing his actual duties at the office on the led April, so that it might be taken that the defendant acquiesced in the work that had been done by the plaintiff from the first of the month, which carried out the condition of a clause in the agreement. Providing that the eng-,ge: ment was to cominance on the first day of April.-.Mr:' Harper : -The duplicate agreement says the fourth.—Hisi Honour (reading from tbe agreement): As and from the first day of April. 1887.—Mr. Harper :. The duplicate in the possession of defendant, and containing plaintiff's signature, says the "fourth" April.—Mr. Jenkins said. that plaintiff's agreement, signed by the defendant, said the "first" of April, and, was admitted.— ' HisHonour: There has been an erasure,and it is not initialled —Mr Harper said that it • was a most extraordinary die- crepancv, and affected practically theonly point in dispute. The only agreement he had seen was the one with the words "Fourth Arrril." He thought the "fourth" in the agree- ment is'in the handwriting of the plaintiff himself. —Mr Jenkins: Here is an agreement signed by the defendant with the words "first "of April.—His Honour: And one, signed by the plaintiff, in which the word "fourth " is put.—Mr. Harper: I am prepared to prove that the worde "fourth " of April are in the handwriting of the plaintiff.— Mr Jenkins proceeded yr say that plaintiff continued his duties for about ten' weeks, when defendant made some complaint as to the number of advertisementa he bad expected,not being obtained. So further corn. plaint was made, and matters went on until the expiration of the three calendar months, which was on the 30th of Jima. On that date the plaintiff, not being satisfied with his position, gave his employer notice as follows. • " let July, 1887. Dear Mr. Hall I beg to give you three months' notice of my intention to vacate the position I bold as editor of the "Barleatown Guardian."—His Hon- our : That all depends upon the question of the date.—Mr. Jenkins: I contend that the agreement commenced on the Ist April, as expressed by the one signed by the defendant. Proceeding, Mr. Jenkins satd that on the 2nd July defend- ant served a notice on the plaintiff informing him that the engagement terminated at the end of three months, reckon- ing from the 4th April, as in his (defendant's) opinien, plaintiff had failed to carry oat the provisions of the agreement in regard to promoting the interests of the paper. He (Mr. Jenkins) understood Mr. Harper withdrew any ha-. imitation of inefficiency.—Mr. Harper said it would not be necessary to enter into that. The engagement, be conten- ded, was an experimental one fer three months, and Mr. Hall was within his rights in terminating it.—Mr. Jenkins contended that that was not the ;honer construction to be put on the agreement. But, if that construction was put upon it, he submitted that there he been a renewal of the engagement.—His .ITo4our : It all depends whether the agreement runs from the fourth or the first.—Plaintiff then gave evidence in support of his claim. Referring to the date of fourth April, he said that he had all along thought that the agreement commenced OR the first, and bad quite , forgotten about the introduction of the word "fourth," which was undoubtedly in his handwriting.—Mr Harper pointed out that plaintiff accepted one week's salary on the Satur- day following the fourth of April, whereas if he had com- menced his duties on the Ist he would have been entitled to payment for ten days. It was apparent that at that time Mr. Hall thought the duties commenced on the fourth, and 'that Mr. Jones acquiesced. He submitted that no notice was necessary to determine an agreement at the end of, "three months certain,* and be was willing to rest his case ,ntirely upon the fact that before the termination of the three months defendant had given plaintiff to understand ,that he should not remain beyond the three months.—His Honour, saying that he should like to look further into the law with regard to the variation in the agreements, reserved his decision.

Sir.—ln :emir L ndoa I;t-te-l-pt-itTli&d lest Saturday I find toe fellowing in reference to a play named "A Mid- summer Nisht's Dream The performance was origin illy arranged for Saturday afternoon, hut as all the world will be at the Naval iieview, it has been found necessary to alter the date. The olay will be presented on Sundav in the eveninu. not in the afternoon. The moon was invited, but had an eng.esment elsewhere, and the scene will accor- dingly be illuminated by the electric light." I wish 0 ask, when may we expect the Theatre and the Publ.c Hell to be opened on Sunday nights for the people to enjoy themselves in like manner. PAUL PRY.

MR. DIGGLE AND THE INTERCEPTING DEPTS. need hardly say that I do not agree with Mr. Diggle when he refers to people who wf te letters over a nom.de.yume as "carping cowards." When writing letters to a newspaper there are a variety of circumstances to be taken into account. We preanme that when anyone writes a letter to a newspaper he has some ideas he wishes to con- vey to the public, or some statement or proposition to make. In dealing with the matter of signatures a man naturally i considers wkether his words will carry more weight if he signs his own name, or if they will be mire likely to effeCt their purpose if he does not connect them with his own personality. If the writer is, or thinks he is, a man of standing and position, he will, no doubt, generally subscribe his own name, hat if, on the other hand, he is modest and does not think hinuolf of any particular account, he will probably think it better to depend upon the intrinsic merits of what he has to say and adopt a nom-de- plume. When Mr. Diagle wrote his letter about the inter- captiag cl2p,ts he acted injudiciously in not keeping these circumstances in mind. Even he cannot have per- suaded himself Oat he is a man of standing and position, yet he appended his own name to his letter, and in this way connected his own individuality with the subject of the letter. The certain result of this would he that the letter would not have as much eff:mt as it &et otherwise have had. I have no doubt whatever that a considerable number of people would while reading the letter think it looked rather bad for the intercepting depots, but on coming to the signature the whole effact would at once disappear. They would probably say, Oh, it's only Diggle • Digarle's al- ways mare-nestimr," and think nothing more ;bout it. Mr. Diggie seems to think it courageous of a writer to put his own name to his leVer, but he mast know that there are other virtues beeides courage. DiEcretion is commonly re- garded to be a higher virtue than courage, and I think it comes to this, after all, that Mr. Digatle has courage and I have discretion. Mr. Diggle courageonely sets down his name, and, as ha is notoriously addicted t.) fads, spoiled the effect of his letter, while your other correspondent and I, not considering ourselves of any particular account, and not led away by ridiculous vanity, were discreet enough to allow whit we had to say to at and or fall on its own merits. .--Yours, S. M.

THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION. Sir,—l notice in last Saturday's " Examiner " that "Clifford Dix " honours me with a friendly criticism of my speech at a iecmt open-air temperance meeting. If your correspondent is sincere in his professe4 sympathy for or movement (which I very much doubt) I would invite, him to throw (If the mask of an anonymous writer and to append his name. If he will do this I will undertkke to prove the correctness of every sentiment I uttered in my address. I cannot consent to discuss with anonymous writers, the temperance cause; our work is to greet, our opportunities are so few, and time is so precioum.—Yours truly, WILLIAM ROBERTS.
Sir,—lt is a rematicable sign of the times, and of the fact
that "God's grace" is resting on the temperance movement,

- - that no one now ventsres to opposetemperance work by word or deed, without calling himself a "friend of temperance." The cause is, thank God, slowly becoming fashionable. Temperance werkers may, however, be excused front con- sidering those as real friends of the movement who only shew their friendship by words tending to disparage the work that is being done. Let Mr." Clifford Dix" vend a a year or two in earnest temperance work and we will rever- ently list.-n to hie criticisms as TO a friend of temperance. With regard to the medical aspect of the (petition to which Mr. " Clifford Dix" refers, " teetotallers " prefer to take the opinion of those who have mule alcohol a sped il study (e.g , Ike. Richardson, Norman Kerr, Alfred Carpen- ter, dm.) to that of those medical men who accept without inquiry the old-fashioned opinions which modern science is daily showing to be more and more erroneous. Perhaps if Mr." Clifford Dix" were to study the ivritings of theee gentlemen he might be induced to cenclude that it is no more desirable to take" a glass of XX " for" hi a stomach's sake" than to partake of oil "to make him a cheerful coon- tenence," or indeed to be bl-d hy 9 surgeon for every trifling ailment. Tempora mutantur et ?WS mutamur in itlis! A word io reference to the speech of Mr. Roberts Of the distribution of foablic-boumes in Warrington, I am not cempetent to speak, having an insufficient knowledge of the locality. London, however, would amply bear out the opinion that" there aiways seems to be the largest number of public-housea amongst the poorest part of the popula- tion." I once bad soup of London, with every publichouse marked In. red, which proved it conclusively. With regard to his ether statement that " there is more drunkenness amongst the poirer portion of the population than iri any other section of the community," perhaps my Owo opinion may be of BCtiThi weight. I write from personal knowledge, having worked in a flahi, noble West End parish, before coming to Warrington, which had also a large spriuk•

lieg of abject poor. That drunkenness is confined to the poor, I will never admit. The evil permeates every claret ef h 1 society. and I know of cases in which even titled people i \ ' have fallen victims to intemperance. Hence the nemssitV i of the " gospei " of the Federation that total abstinence is ' the sateet and wisest course for all. But my own experi- \ ence and that of much older workers than myself tends to I show that it is from the poorer classes that the ranks of the drunkards are mainly filled. Nor is the reason far to seek. , 'rho poor are not more vicious than the rich, hut the drink ' makes them poor first and then criminal. They are lowered in the social scale in the process of de4radation. Hence these wealthy brewers, who wax fat oa the vices of their poorer brethien, plant their pablic-hous,s (in Louie* at all events) where they will do the most prosperous trade, namely in the haunts of poverty—Yours faithfully, J. J. LANGHANI, Hon. Sec. Warrington Temperance Federation.

_ . Site—The arguments out forward by our teetotal friends seem to be of a twofold character. They urge that the use of intoxicatirg liquors is at the root of our evils, or perhaps I should say all our evils ; and further' in the words of Richadson that "the iluration of life in this country was diminished to the extent of one third through the sale and use of intoxicating liquors." With the first of these propositions there is an almost universal disagreement ; quality the statement and it may be accepted. As thus— the crime and misery which is stalking through our midst for desolate homes, bruised husbands, beaten women, and starvine children, we chiefly look to drink as the cause—the immoderate and criminal use of alcohol. But now. I ask, is it only with the poor workman in his dingy, stifimg dwelling that you find the abuse of strong drink? Lady John Manners In her sketch of "Rich men's dwellings," gives such details of the lives of those who pre slime to lecture the masses that I must be excused for giv- ing cne or two instances to your readers. Taking the daily life in a Scotch shooting lodge she save—" Before most of the gentlemen leave their beds they fortify them- selves with brandy and soda." Champagne, whiskey, and claret are sent to the fields for the sportmen's use, while as a "happy thought of his own, he carries a mixture of curacoa and brandy in his flask." ' Before retiring to rest" brews of many kinds are prepared—effervescing waters, whiskey, brandy, claret, lemons in profusion must be at hand; so many men, so many tastes." And it is well-knewn that this is not a strained description of the life rich men lead. Lord Brat:emelt states that "It never seems to enter the heads of rich people that there can be any ether choice of life before them than that of an idler" ; sect we all know what that means. If not, the police and divorce court re- cords are wasted. There is abundance of evidence of debauchery and drun- kenness amongst the upper cl Issas. The Archdeacon of Warrington in a sermon the other day said :—"They were told that they must tot condemn the licensing of debau- chery, and the allowing women to he destroyed that men might elloy their damnable lusts. The same was the case at home when the church buckled on her arrnoua to deal with the home heathen who were to be found among the rich merchants of our great cities and the highest society in the west end of London. The clergy were told that how- ever they might speak of the vices of the messes they must not mention those of the classes, for a peer's robe, like charity, covers a multitude of sins." I give these extracts to prove that there is not "mere drunkenness among the poorer portion of the population than in any other sec- tion of the community,* It may be further insisted that the degradation through drink, of the poorer classes, is seen of all the world. No tips can relieve them of the magistrates sneers, or the tra- ditional "5s and costs." No, their degradation is complete and above board, while that of the more favoured ones is hidden in club life, with well trained fienkies to see that a cab is always at hand. Mr. Tonge must know that nothing increases the difficul- ties of young men just starting in life, even as ministers, so much as the strong temptations held out at the rich man's table to take wine. I cannot, and do not, offer the above as an excuse for the drinking habits of the poor, but I may he allowed to point out, that if the more fa- voured ones can drink to excess, surely there is some ex- cuse for the leas favoured ones. Question any Doctor with a large and fashionahle practice as to the tippling and consumption of scientific mixtures amongst his patients, and what will the answer be? I know, and could, from etatements new before MP, give startling evi- dence as to how our pastors and masters conduct them- selves when within their own charmed circle, but enough, let US look for a remedy. Lord B abozan in his "Appeals to men of leisure," states that "never was there greater separation between rich and poor, never was personal work amonget the poor, and suffering, in body or in epirir, more needed than at present." Lord Cranborne (son of Lord Salisbury), speak- ing in Lancashire, in September, 1885, said, " the Conser- vatives would do very wrong were they to deceive the people with false hopes ; misery, poverty, and inequality, are the heritage of mankind." Taking the latter state- ment for all it is worth, OF as representing a state of things as unalterable as the laws of the Medea; and Persians, what is likely to he the result of Lord Brabnan's eff arts. or the pereeverieg work of the Temperance party ? Surely labour in vain. But is it not possible for our temperance friends, during their walks around School Brow Town's End, or the Factory Yard to fancy themselves sinking in- to the veriest drunkards, were they obliged to pate their Byes in such routers? Fancy a man passing eight or nine bourn in a forge, coal pit, glass house, or a factory, and seeking his heaven in these soul-killing districts! I grant there are exceptions, that men do resist drink under all these unf tvourable awe's, but I attk that the workers he dealt with as all experience claims they should be dealt with. There is a vast difference between leaving a Wiling mill, and a well-ventilated office ; so there is a vast difference between the home of the mill hand, and his gill of fourpeeny, and the well-paid secretary or director, and his bottle of wino. Make It Impossible for any man to reap a profit from another man'e misery. Is it not true that the poorest and filthiest property is the best paying? The poorest house in Warrington yields a higher per oentage than the best ' built mansion on the Cheshire bill side. Again, in their strivings with the publicans, the teeto- I tallers are all at see. Free trade in drink is the secret of the gnestien. Repeal indirect taxation, allow any man to brew, or sell beer and spirits, tags the money "turn-over" that State taxation gives to the liquor traffic, and it would I cease to pay any man to deface street corners with gin 'palaces. It is well known that the two brewers in War- rington, whom the Queen has delighted to honour, are pur- chasing every license that'comee in the marker. regardless of Cost. Why allow this monopoly to go on any longer? As I have said before, make it impossible for a man to get riches out of his fellow man's weakness, and success will surely follow. At the present time the personal interests of most of the me.ohers of Peril ament are at one with the great brewers, distillers, and the shoal of publicans and sinners of all grades. A further statement may be made as a fact that is. that the people will nevor become al-strainers We know that the chances of * long life ore more favourable in our day then that of our fathers. If ale kills, it kills slowly, when taken in moderation, therefore make the public house what it ought Cr be—a house of entertainment, and for refresh- ment. Take away its peculiar caste features, the taproom, and the bar parlour ; let it be knnwn that it is as respect- able as any' ether business place, and that a man loses nothing by falling his wife or his daoghter there, as they do en the continent; let all classes, and both sexes have the privilege and opportunity of meeting for social and reasonable intercourse,and the degrading talk, and worse than beastly state which men and women unfortunately lapse into will be for ever done away with. CLIFFORD DIX.
BATHING FATALTTV AT WIDNER.-GALLANT
CONDUCT OF A BOY.

Mr. S. Brighouse, the coroner, on Tuesday held an inquest at Widnes, to inquire into the circumstances at- tending the drowning of William Thomas. 15 years of age, son of Henry Thomas, labourer, of 15, Violet-street. Widnes. Robert Thomas, 13 years of age, said the deceased wis his brother, and together with several other boys they on Satur- day went to a piece of waste land, off Moor-lane, to play cricket. On the return journey they came to a nit of water and the deceased boasted bow he could swim in the baths, and said he would go into the water. His companions tried to persuade him not to do so, and at the request of the de- ceased witness jumped into the water and swam across. The deceased then undressed himself. and despite the efforts of those present, entered the water and attempted to swim rcross. After taking one or two strokes be threw up his arms and cried "save me," and then sank. One of the boys named James Cadman dived to the rescue of the de- ceased, but could not reach him before he sank for th- last time.—ln answer to a question witness said he did not know that his brother could swim. He bad never seen him in water before. The water of the pit was not very cold, but it was very deep ; lads often bathed in it. He thought his brother was seized with cramp.—James Cadman, 15 years of age, who lives in Victoria-road, gave corroborative evidence. He said that when he saw the deceased drowning he pulled off his clothes and cut his shoe laces so that he could bare his feet quicker. He then plunged into the water, and had made twe or three strtires when the deceased came up for the last time. lie made a " grab "at him, and he was within three inches of reaching his band. The deceased sank, and he (witness) came out of t.ho water. In renly to the coroner Cadman said it was not long sloes he learned to swim. He could swim three quarters of the length of the baths.—Mr. A. Parkes (a jurym rn) said great credit was due to Cadman tor his conduct. —Another jury- man said that had Calman grasped the hand r‘f the de- ceased the latter would have nulled him down, and both would have been drowned.—P.C. Worsfold deposed to re- covering the body with drags. The pit was at least 12 feet deep. and was 15 or 18 feet wide. There was a good number of old trees in the pit, and it had a very dangerous look. Anyone that went in it would be very courageous. The sides went straight down. From the appearance of the deceased he was of opinion he bad been seized with cramp, —ln answer to the Coroner, Sergeant Clarkson said persons on the land where the pit was were trespassers.—The Groner said the only verdict that could be returned was accidental death. At the :same time if they thought Cad. man's conduct deserving of recounition they could say so, and he would embody it in the verdict, and forward it to the proper quarter. Personally he thought that Cadman being only 15 years of age, and rooly able to swim a shot distance, and the pit having a forbidding appearance, it was very courageous on his part to attempt to rescue the deceased.—The jury returned a yordi3t of " Accidental Death," and expressed a high opinion of the gallant con- duct of Cadman in attempting to save his friend. RUNCORN'S " kir-RATE POET" SENT TO THE ASYLUM.

At Runcorn Police Court, -01-1-7rh-traday, before Mr. G. L. Davies. James Herringshaw. aged 55 years, was broug..t up in custody charged with being a wandering lunatic. The prisoner, who lived at a lodging-house in Mersey-street • was apprehended by P.C. May on Wednesday night. He was "raving" about the ship cinal, and was wearing at the time a number of what ha called "Ship C mat Medals." He was also decorated with ribbons. Dr. McDougall certi- fied that the man was insane. The prisoner informed the re igistrate that he was the person who took up the Ship I Canal Scheme, and who bad been instrumental in the Rill being carried. He bad been to Liverpool. and he said the people there were going to murder him for the active part be had taken in passing the Bill. The magistrate ordered Rerringshaw to be removed to Chester Lunatic Asylum. On leaving the police station for his mew abode, "Jemmy" called for three cheers for the Ship Canal. Far a great number of years the poor fellow has been in the habit of singing (?) original songs (?) in the street on topics of passing interest, and for a long period wore upon his breast a large medal made of tin, bearing the inscription " Grate Runcorn Poet." This, he said, bad been presented to him by Mr. John Bright. He was un- usually excited by the Ship Canal Scheme, and during the past three year., all his " poetry !" has been in reference tc it. The townsp-ople permated his vagaries wilh amused tolerance, but lately " Jemmy " has become rather violent in his actions, and it has been found necessary to remove him to the asylum.

Busi• ness is a misnomer for there is no busy-ness in Throgmorton Street and the eutside speculator is, for the moment, non-ex- istent as far as the city is concerned. In the absence of the British public, stocke are tumbling down all round Home Rails perhaps more than any. Brighton as the most ' sensitive are down in spite of improved traffics and will I probably go lower yet, so that the investor, who buys to held, will have the greater cause for rejoicing hereafter, bate course he should not buy on a felling market. Russian 73's are up a trifle in spite of the continued unload- ' ing in Berlin, but it is only the spasmodic struggles that I herald the cessation of effort. The promoters of the Edgbasten (Birmingham) Brewery Company are endeavouring to hurry uptinvestors by a notice that applications for shares most be sent in by baturday. There is little doubt that the promoters would be very glad I to be in a poeition to decline applications made after that I date, but they are hardly likely to be in a poeition to do so. With a capital of £lOO,OOO in shares of £l. each, a com- pany has been formed to acquire the patent rights of a new I invention in fire lighting, under the title of the Paten* Champion Fire Lighter, Limiled. The demand is expect-d to be so enormous that, after careful consideration, the di• rectors calculate one dividen,d of 30 per cent. The Cheshire Alkali Company, Limited, is formed with a cepital of £300,000, in shares of £5 each, divided into 46.000 preference 7 per cent. and 14,000 deferred shares. The objects of the company are to work patents, mere especially improvements of Dr. Pick, by the ammonia-soda process. It is stated that the vendor has so much confi dence in the undertaking that be has agreed to accept all his purchase money in deferred shares. The list of appli- cations close on Wednesday. August 3rd, for town, and Thursday, August 4th, tot the country.

During the past twelve months Mr. Verdin prac- tically devoted the whole of his time to his Parlia- mentary duties, and there is no doubt that the long hours of the House of Commons had a most preju- dicial effect upon his health. In the night of Wed- nesday the 13th he had a severe spasmodic attack at his hotel, and was seen by Drs. Poore and Pye- Smith, of London. He rallied, and attended to his Parliamentary work lill Saturday morning, July 16th, when he returned home and was attended by Dr. Joynson, of Northwich, under *hose treatment he seemed to improve. By his friends his case was considered critical, but strong hopes of his recovery were entertained, even to the last. He went on favourably tilt four o'clock on the Wednesday morn- ing, when another spasm of the heart prostrated him. Dr. Joynson was sent for, and remained with him the -whole of the day.. A telegram, announcing his illness, was sent to Winsford, while the Jubilee festivities were in progress, and caused great regret. Mr. Verdin recovered from his attack, and was go- ing on well when there was another, but less severe seizure wi Friday evening. On Saturday morning. Sir William Roberts, of Manchester, was sent for, and saw the patient in consultation with Mr. Joyn- son. He regarded the case as one of extreme gravi-, ty, needing perfect quietness and rest. BAsin OF HOPE UNION.—The annual gide in con- nection with the Warrington Band of Hope Union is to take place next Mondayein the field adjoining St James' Church, Wilderspool Causeway. A DRUNKEN FREAK.—At Daresbury Petty Ses- sions, on Tuesday morning, a young man named William Crook, residing at Crowton, was summoned for having stolen three egg cups and two salt cel- lars, the property of Mary Ann Cowap, from the Horns Inn, Little Leigh. It was alleged that a man named Jones saw defendant put his arm through the pantry window from the outside and take the articles mentioned. On an alarm being raised he dropped the articles and ran off, and they were picked up by the proprietor and Jones. Crook stated he was so drunk that lie did not remember anything about it; and Roger Tickle, whom he called as a witness, stated that Crook was so drunk at ten o'clock that night in a field belonging to Mrs Cowap that he was unable to go home, and he also laid down beside him and slept till four o'clock next; morning. (Laughter.)—The Chairman, addressing defendant, said they had no desire, nor did they wish to convict him of felony, because it would be a slur on his whole life; when he committed the Offence he was probably enjoying himself too much, but that was no excuse. The case would be dis- missed, but at the same time they would instruct the police to summon him( next Court day for being drunk.

LOCAL TRADSSICRN AND THE RAILWAY Ca:— An acl• journed meeting of local tradesmen to receive the report of rtre deputation appointed at a meeting held last week, as stated in our last issue, to wait upon the railway company in references to grievances in regard to the unloading and delivery of goods at the Earlestosn goods department, was to have been held in Mr. Clarke's room, Bridge-street, op fuesday evening. Owing to other meetings in the town the attendance was only small, and no formal meeting was held. It was stated, however, that the deputation had waited upon Mr. Braids, the goods traffic manager, as the representative r f the railway company, and he promised to bring the matter before the directors.
